## 1 - CIP vs CRC

Regarding _"CIP - specific changes to the protocol that all nodes would need to agree on and adopt (if approved)"_

I am afraid that this is simply _impossible_ because the CIP process isn't authoritative, but in a way is only an opt-in process. No one can force a node implementer to _follow a particular CIP_, unless that particular CIP is part of the protocol. We historically tried to have CIP be authoritative; and it didn't work because it's the wrong vehicle for *enforcing* decisions. 

So, in effect, CIPs are much closer to "community standards, best practices, etc." at this point; though some also contain specific solutions that have become or can become protocol features (think about CIP-0031, CIP-0032, CIP-0033 or CIP-0138 for example).

I strongly disagree with the idea that CIPs shouldn't contain implementation details. They SPECIFICALLY should. That's the intended purpose of a CIP; to be detailed enough that it can be implemented. A specification may leave room for implementation choices, but it may certainly specify constraints, expected behavior and very low-level details such as binary formats. 

## 2 - CIP Editors

Regarding  having "CIP editors [who] would be more knowledgable about the core technical components of the node"; I think it's a misunderstanding of the role of CIP editors here. Editors aren't (necessarily, although they can be) technical experts in the room. They are the guardian of the CIP Process. The role of an editor is to ensure that the process is diligently followed; and they help coordinate and facilitate reviews around CIPs.  

The _reviewers_ are the experts. And so far, it's always been a permissionless process. Wanna be a reviewer? Take a shovel and go provide feedback! 

## 3 - CIP  Improvement Proposal (CIPIP :D)

I only have one suggestion regarding improving the CIP process, which is to start thinking about having more diverse category champions for specific categories: ledger, plutus, consensus & network. By "diverse", I mean having people from different node workstreams. Although, it's important to keep in mind that:

1.  We cannot _force_ people to be champions if they don't want to;
2. I do feel that the current Plutus or Ledger champions are quite receptive to feedback and are very proactive in seeking expert opinions outside of their own teams when needed -- and I see a large overlap between CIP reviewers (occasional or recurring ones) and node implementers anyway. 

So, it's also not _a problem_ per se. I think the CIP process is fine and work _as intended_ for that purpose. What could however need improvement and/or formalisation is the layer coming _after_ the CIP process: how do we collectively decide and agree on the technical roadmap of Cardano and what it means to be "a cardano node". That privilege has so far been the one of IOG, which seems to be willing to share it with a broader community (judging by recent social media posts and initiatives such as the node diversity workshop and the blueprint project). 

My "dream" would be that moving forward:

- ANY protocol (which includes the ledger rules, consensus algorithm and any observable changes in the networking interfaces) is first specified and discussed as a CIP. 
- There exists _another process_ for "bundling" CIPs together into milestones for Cardano. That process should ensure proper scoping, non-functional requirements such as performance targets, budget and approval of node implementers -- and ultimately, of DReps through the means of an Info Action (basically preceding and announcing a future hard fork).   
- Once finalized and fully implemented, ensure that any change to the protocol is reflected in the Cardano blueprint project (not to be mixed up with CIP-0057!).

This way, the CIP can remain a place for technical solutions that have received some level of feedback and can be the go-to place for node implementers for (a) discussing/proposing technical changes and (b) seeking for guidelines/best practices. 

The bargaining on the roadmap and authoritative aspects of which CIPs shall make it into the roadmap is best done separately from CIPs, as another layer with different processes and people.

> I am afraid that this is simply impossible because the CIP process isn't authoritative, but in a way is only an opt-in process.

In this case "specific changes to the protocol that all nodes would need to agree on and adopt (if approved)" is simply shorthand for "suggestions about specific changes to the protocol that all nodes would need to agree on and adopt for them to be effective, which can then be fed into a more authoritative process like on-chain governance". I'm trying to draw the distinction between CIPs that are only practical / worthwhile if they *do* reach a broad and authoritative consensus, and those that are useful regardless. For an example of this distinction, think reference scripts vs governance metadata. One is useless unless a plurality of nodes implement and hard fork to deploy it ("hard consensus"), the other just announces something that one or more people intend to do, and would be convenient if more people did consistnetly ("soft consensus").

I'm certainly not trying to make the CIP process authoritative for exactly the same reasons you outline.

> I strongly disagree with the idea that CIPs shouldn't contain implementation details.

Everything you outline in the rest of this paragraph is things that I don't think of as "implementation details". 😅  Certainly taking a literal definition, things like CBOR formats are details of an implementation. But usually we use the term "implementation details" to refer to the things that are outside of the concern of the interface. Something is "just an implementation detail" because it's internal to the function, and not something the caller needs to be concerned about.

So, yes, I'm arguing that CIPs should contain the interface boundary: CDDL specs for binary formats, expected behavior, etc; but the details of how to implement that behavior (what you call "implementation choices") are more suggestions / reference implementations / etc. that don't need the kind of "hard consensus" I describe above that an on-the-wire binary format would need.

> There exists another process for "bundling" CIPs together into milestones for Cardano. That process should ensure proper scoping, non-functional requirements such as performance targets, budget and approval of node implementers -- and ultimately, of DReps through the means of an Info Action (basically preceding and announcing a future hard fork).

This is a similar process to the one that Ori outlined at the node diversity workshop that Ethereum uses. And that's why I think dividing CIPs and CRCs would be beneficial: the "set of things" that that new authoritative process needs to haggle over, vs the things where the "authoritative process" is more about ecosystem adoption and organic competition.

I will say, as the potential author of many CIPs over the last 4 years, the lack of this distinction has been the major psychological deterrent for me. > I am afraid that this is simply _impossible_ because the CIP process isn't authoritative, but in a way is only an opt-in process. No one can force a node implementer to _follow a particular CIP_, unless that particular CIP is part of the protocol. We historically tried to have CIP be authoritative; and it didn't work because it's the wrong vehicle for _enforcing_ decisions.

This is part of why my initial idea involved an entirely new process, so we don't bring along any "CIP baggage" that may exist. That being said, I think that of _course_ any off chain consensus solution is not authoritative, because we cannot control what anyone does in the network. However, I _do_ think they can become "de facto" authoritative. What I mean by that is if enough of the node maintainers participate in the new consensus solution, it becomes the solution for Cardano. Of course I expect disagreements and people to break off–just look at Intersect–but, generally, my vision was having each hard fork change log simply be a list of "CIP-like" documents describing the ledger changes (or consensus, or networking). None of it is forceful, Cardano is what is actually running on the network with more than 51% stake. But, in practice, I believe the node implementors can come together around this because it makes everyone's lives easier.


> So, in effect, CIPs are much closer to "community standards, best practices, etc." at this point; though some also contain specific solutions that have become or can become protocol features (think about CIP-0031, CIP-0032, CIP-0033 or CIP-0138 for example).
I think this is a part of the "CIP baggage" I mentioned. Step away from the existing CIPs and consider what I'm proposing in terms of "specifications that define and explain changes to the protocol."

> I strongly disagree with the idea that CIPs shouldn't contain implementation details. They SPECIFICALLY should. That's the intended purpose of a CIP; to be detailed enough that it can be implemented. A specification may leave room for implementation choices, but it may certainly specify constraints, expected behavior and very low-level details such as binary formats.
Pi said my piece, but I'll echo that "implementation details" is another overloaded term. We should define an interface and expected behavior, but you should not tell me how my software reaches that point. For example, Amaru is handling validation very differently than the Haskell node, but we're (hopefully?) coming to the same conclusion.

> Regarding having "CIP editors [who] would be more knowledgable about the core technical components of the node"; I think it's a misunderstanding of the role of CIP editors here. Editors aren't (necessarily, although they can be) technical experts in the room. They are the guardian of the CIP Process. The role of an editor is to ensure that the process is diligently followed; and they help coordinate and facilitate reviews around CIPs.
> 
> The _reviewers_ are the experts. And so far, it's always been a permissionless process. Wanna be a reviewer? Take a shovel and go provide feedback!
I think you're stuck in the existing framework of a CIP. I would agree that the CIP editors are simply guardians of the process, not the dictators of it. But there are two points:
1) There are fewer external reviewers in practice. From what I've seen, often the editors _are_ the reviewers.
2) Having buy-in from node implementors would make reaching consensus around the protocol much easier. Obviously, it can't be required, but if a node wanted to have a say in the future of the protocol, they better get involved.

Ultimately, none of this is possible without the buy-in of the Haskell team at the moment. They are dictators of the network (I don't mean that in a bad way, but in the sense that whatever software they push, we have to follow) at the moment. They could totally ignore this process, until someone comes along and replaces that software in the network. Once we reach sufficient node decentralization, participation would be "required", otherwise you'd just fork off into the abyss (or into something else?).

That is exactly the reason I think a new process for coming to consensus on managing the protocol would really work. Unlike current CIPs, which are largely usage standards such as CIP-30, either you implement Cardano, or you implement something Cardano-like. And once there is a diverse node ecosystem, no one party could force the network in any direction.

> My "dream" would be that moving forward:
> 
> * ANY protocol (which includes the ledger rules, consensus algorithm and any observable changes in the networking interfaces) is first specified and discussed as a CIP.
> * There exists _another process_ for "bundling" CIPs together into milestones for Cardano. That process should ensure proper scoping, non-functional requirements such as performance targets, budget and approval of node implementers -- and ultimately, of DReps through the means of an Info Action (basically preceding and announcing a future hard fork).
> * Once finalized and fully implemented, ensure that any change to the protocol is reflected in the Cardano blueprint project (not to be mixed up with CIP-0057!).
> 
> This way, the CIP can remain a place for technical solutions that have received some level of feedback and can be the go-to place for node implementers for (a) discussing/proposing technical changes and (b) seeking for guidelines/best practices.
> 
> The bargaining on the roadmap and authoritative aspects of which CIPs shall make it into the roadmap is best done separately from CIPs, as another layer with different processes and people.

It sounds like we agree. I am simply proposing that we define a framework around this process that solidifies it. If it doesn't work out, it doesn't work out and we figure something else out. I just think you have to step outside the "what is the CIP process" box and think about how we could start from scratch. Once we know that, it's much easier to figure out how to modify the existing process to fit our needs.

And let me just add: I understand the framing of "stop thinking about CIPs" in the CIPs repository may be a bit strange and perhaps even hostile. That is certainly not the goal. I just think we have a unique opportunity in front of us in which we are about to experience a seismic shift in the network with node diversity and we have an opportunity to drop our "process debt" and start with a clean slate.

I love the CIP process. I think it is one of the most important pieces of Cardano. And, I believe we can do better for protocol upgrades in particular.

> I disagree. Why would the cache store failing scripts? A transaction with a script that fails in phase 2 consumes collateral, which can of-course be costed higher than a legitimate transaction (and should be, because there is no reason any honest actor would ever submit such a transaction).

The cache has to store failing scripts because the attack gets even easier if it doesn't. Remember that cache misses are the issue here, and so if I know my scripts aren't going to be cached I can just do many transactions with exactly the same scripts.

And yes, you could not cache the scripts and charge a higher collateral that makes up for this difference. That means that you're now moving the complexity from the fee calculation to the collateral calculation. This is a bit nicer for the users because the actual fees are lower, but it doesn't actually make things easier.

Another issue is that you can also do this attack with succeeding scripts. I don't know how viable it is, but I'm sure you could write some tooling that finds scripts on mainnet that you can use for your attack. So if this attack is viable and there are enough honest scripts that you can abuse then all of these optimizations won't save you.

I'm okay with changing the name, but I don't think `Guard` is a great name. The reason that I gave the title Observe is because this is the only script type which does not directly correspond to "guarding" a given ledger action. All existing script types correspond to and "guard" a given ledger action. Observation scripts is in-fact the only script type which doesn't "guard" anything. 

Spending -> guards the spending of a UTxO at a script address
Minting -> guards the minting/burning of tokens of a currency symbol 
Rewarding -> guards the withdrawal of rewards from a script stake account
Certifying -> guards the registration / deregistration / delegation of a script stake credential
Voting -> guards the voting of a script DRep / CCM
Proposing -> guards parameter change and treasury withdrawal governance actions.
Observing -> guards no action

Every other script type is REQUIRED for a transaction with a corresponding ledger action to be valid, they all guard those actions. Observer scripts on their own do not actually guard anything; they don't correspond to any ledger action at all. The exact same transaction (in terms of impact on ledger state) can be valid with or without an observation script. It is only through other scripts that they "guard" things. 

An example is spending scripts forwarding their validation logic to an observation script. In this case, a spending script that is guarding the spending of a UTxO at a script address, has logic to check that a given observation script is present. The spending script is what is actually guarding, the observation script is just making an observation, in this case, it just so happens that the guarding logic of the spending script enforces that a given observation must be made.

> The only reason to include such a script in a transaction is for other scripts (which are triggered by transaction components) to delegate their validation logic to it. Moreover, the transaction can't succeed validation unless this script successfully executes.

This is not true. There are valid use-cases where an observation script is included even when it's not required by other scripts, to simply make a verified observation about the transaction. This is especially relevant for cross-chain interoperability protocols, L2 interop, bridging, and BTC-DeFi. 

> Moreover, the transaction can't succeed validation unless this script successfully executes.

Strictly speaking yes, that exact serialized transaction cannot succeed unless the script successfully validates, however, that is a property that is not unique to observation scripts, that is true of every script type supported by Cardano. Importantly, while the exact serialized tx cannot succeed, a transaction which has an identical impact on the ledger state (same UTxOs spent, same outputs produced, same rewards withdrawn, same credentials registered, etc) can indeed succeed without the inclusion of an observation script, unless that observation script is required by some other script which actually guards ledger state transitions.

> Every other script type is REQUIRED for a transaction with a corresponding ledger action to be valid

If a script hash is supplied in the transaction, then it is also REQUIRED, so I don't see you point.
Observation implies it cannot affect the outcome of transaction validation, which is not true.

> Observer scripts on their own do not actually guard anything; 

I respectfully disagree with this. They guard a transaction as a whole. If a script fails, then the whole transaction will be considered as phase2 invalid, just like any other plutus script in a transaction.

I could agree that addition to the native script `RequireObserver` can be viewed as an observer, since all it does is observing that the required script has been added to required scripts necessary for validation. However, this feature is not limited to native scripts and any arbitrary plutus can be included, which does not necessarily depend on any other scripts in a transaction, thus acting as transaction guarding script.

Hello, party pooper here, can someone please remind me what nested transactions allow that is not already possible?

For how I see it, this proposal is trying to fill the gap with PSBT on bitcoin, where I remind you there is no turing complete scripting feature. As a result, most of the applications on bitcoin are inherently centralized.

In my point of view, this CIP is equivalent to introducing native scripts after plutus.

Nested Transactions allow someone signing a transaction to certify just the portion they care about, even if that portion alone is an invalid transaction, and allow that to be merged atomically with other similarly signed pieces when settling on the ledger.

Today, you can collect signatures from multiple users for a *complete* transaction, but the coordination required for that makes it challenging and serves as a centralizing force for such designs.

It's also possible to emulate this at the smart contract layer using intent systems, but that introduces inefficiencies and awkward aspects of the UX.

With nested transactions, a user can build their "half" of a transaction they care about, and broadcast that over a gossip network (such as the decentralized pub/sub network that the Mithril team are planning to augment the node with, I forget the CIP number) to find parties willing to satisfy the other half.

This *enables* more decentralization in the design of certain types of applications.

The deficiency or design of a specific feature on another chain, even if they vaguely rhyme when you squint your ears, doesn't really have much bearing as a critique on this design (on a chain where we *do* have turing complete scripting features :sweat_smile:), so I'm not sure of the relevance.

I think it's important to not restrict thinking to the Babel Fees application. @Quantumplation explained it quite nicely, but I'll say it a bit differently: the key feature here is that we want to turn interactive protocols (which require back & forth communication, which in practice would be with a centralized service) into non-interactive ones. the beginWallet URI scheme @francisluz already implemented looks like this:
`web+cardano:addr?amount=1&token=ADA&paymentID=123-ABC&note=abcdedafad`

**What it solves**
- Payments with other tokens than ADA (think USDM)
- Linking payments to offchain data (to link a payment to a shopping cart of whatever)

**What it doesn't solve / Downfalls**
- Transactions with multiple tokens
- Uses a ticker symbol instead of a policyId
- Not using the //payment authority

I think the biggest issue here is the ticker symbol and the centralized whitelists that have to come with it to convert the ticker into a policyId to build the transaction. But: I think we have to abandon the original idea of multiple assets to fit into a payment URL anyways, because while URLs can be quite lengthy today in most modern browsers (up to 10,000 characters or something), the bottleneck is the QR-Code with "only" 300-500 characters before the "scanability" decreases massively, which especially for the use case of providing a slick and quick payment method is a no-go.

If we were to go with policyIds instead of ticker symbols, the overall character length excluding the note/msg field would still perfectly fit within these limitations: 
- Identifier, params and stuff: 43+ Characters
- Amount: 1 to whatever (100bn are still only 12 digits)
- Bech32 Address: 104 Characters 
- PolicyId: 56 Characters
- PaymentID/Note: 32-36 Characters (for UUIDv4 e.g., could be shorter or longer ofc)

I think the dedicated paymentId field is debatable, as long as you can put _some_ metadata into a transaction via URL, we cover a lot of use cases.
 
Given that we've spent another year or so without proper definition of this very rudimentary functionality on Cardano, I'd rather see this moving quickly now and enabling stable coins or Hosky or whatever as possible payment method across the ecosystem instead of looking for the perfect solution while seeing wallets coming up with their own individual solutions, but thats just my take ofc.

Please add the following to the CIP.
```
### Certification Issuers

Certification issuers will mint on-chain certification that will represent the level of certification desired and present evidence of the work done.

Certification issuers are identified by the presence of a node in the `certification_issuers` on-chain linked list, which contains a Policy ID that proves their authenticity, and a datum which uniquely identifies them via their public key hash.  
 
Consensus of existing certification issuers is required to:
1. Add a new certification issuer to the `certification_issuers` linked list.  
2. Remove a certificate issuer from the `certification_issuers` linked list, effectively revoking their license to issue audit certificates.
3. Revoke any audit certificate issued by a revoked certificate issuer.

Individual certificate issuers are able to:
1. Issue new audit certificates.
2. Revoke audit certificates which they have issued.

Importantly, they cannot modify audit certificates which were issued by other certification issuers.


#### Requirements for Certification Issuers

##### Initialization

The `certification_issuers` on-chain linked list will start with an initial list of well-known and established audit firms.

##### Certificate Issuer Application
 
1. The `candidate_list` is an on-chain linked list, in which each node represents an application to become a certificate issuer. To become a certificate issuer, a candidate must submit an application to join the `certification_issuers` on-chain linked list. 
2. The result must include proof of the necessary credentials justifying their capacity to do audits and the number of DApps that they have already audited and any audit reports they have published.
3. New certification issuers can be added to the audit committees list only when a quorum of the existing certification issuers has approved their candidacy (node transfer from candidate list to committee list).
4. In case that their application is rejected, they are only removed from the candidate list.
```

> The naive approach would be to just translate the individual certificates into the old "complex" certificates when constructing a PlutusV3 script context ...

That would be a pretty dangerous route.

Imagine a script that locks a staking credential and relies on presence of this multi-function certificate that can register and delegate at once. If you artificially combine a sequence of two certificates: `[cert_0, cert_1_register_A, cert_2_delegate_A, cert_3]` into `[cert_0, register_and_delegate_A, cert_3]`, you are now having serious issues:
1. Supplying a redeemer for all three `cert_1_register_A`, `cert_2_delegate_A` and `cert_3` is no longer correct, since index in redeemer pointer is off by one
2. Script is executed twice instead of once, unless we hack around it somehow
3. Script will not see what was actually supplied
4. We would inadvertently be preventing a potentially expected behavior, where such order of certificates: `[cert_0, cert_1_register_A, cert_2_delegate_A, cert_3]` was desired by the user, but ledger all of a sudden changed it from underneath them.

Most importantly it would have the opposite result: we would make the ledger implementation more complex with hacks like this, not simpler.

>  then provide both the original certificates and the "translated" certificate(s).

You can't do that, since that implies change to `PlutusV3` script context, which is not allowed.

> I will find some time early this week to write a query to find how many scripts have been executed on mainnet for the "complex" certificates.

The fact that you will be able to find all scripts that rely on such certificate on mainnet today, does not rule out all possible scripts like that from ever existing, because they might not have been used on chain yet. In other words someone could have registered a staking credential without providing the preimage of the hash, because today registration certificate does not require a witness. Also someone could have locked an input with a script that relies on a presence of such certificate, which you will not know until such input is spent and it might not happen for many years to come. So, this information cannot possibly serve as proof that your suggestion is sound.

The reason why we have reward account deposit and minUTxO, is to prevent precisely this attack.

If I have a `GuardCredential`, the witness (whether it is a smart contract credential or a payment credential) is required not just to spend from that address, but to send to what address. This CIP requires new addresses, here's why: For backwards compatibility reasons, any transaction that is valid today should be valid in the future. Since I can make arbitrary outputs at any address (given I have the funds) we cannot break this property. Technically, you can make new addresses by extending the set of possible scripts or public keys, but that doesn't help: hashes are completely opaque when creating outputs, and having to provide pre-images again breaks backwards compatibility. The current version of the CIP does exactly that of course.

So there's a very clear downside to this CIP that needs to be mentioned in the text: every downstream tool needs to implement the new address format, whatever it may end up being. So everyone supporting this should weigh the benefits against this cost.

I agree with @lehins, changing the `Credential` type is not the way to go. The most obvious thing to me would be to change the `BaseAddr` type - include a flag that indicates whether this address needs to witness outputs being created at that address. However, this only works for scripts, and only correctly written ones specifically.

The issue is that you can always change this flag and make an output without restrictions. So for a `KeyHash` credential this flag has zero impact on spendability and so any unwanted funds can still be donated even if it's technically a different address. I'm not sure if people would legally or socially agree that these are different addresses, so it doesn't sound useful. For a `ScriptHash` credential, this problem can be solved by the script inspecting the address of the output being spent and verifying that the flag is in fact set correctly. However, this does still not fully solve the problem since such an invalid output could also be referenced to a different script. So all scripts that rely on referencing also need to check that this flag is set correctly.

Also, note that the issue I just described is also present in the design that's currently provided in this CIP.

I also thought about adjusting the hashes (e.g. by prepending a zero if the flag is set) as a way to solve this problem, but it doesn't work: when spending the output you have to reveal the preimage, and at that point the protection provided by this scheme is lost.

In conclusion, evaluated on a purely technical basis the benefits don't seem very strong (only works for scripts, *all* scripts interacting with these addresses need to do extra validation) while the ecosystem cost (implement new addresses) seems fairly high.

Bonus suggestion: it's possible to make a 'wallet script' that requires signatures to accept funds without any ledger changes (and thus without the ecosystem cost). Make a script with a thread token that stores a list of numbers as the state. When spending an output, check the transaction is signed by the private key of the wallet owner and that the datum of the output is of the form `(n, sig)` where `sig` signs `n` with the same private key (otherwise fail). If `n` is already in the state, the script fails, otherwise it adds `n` to the state.

With that script, anyone can publicly verify what outputs at that script are spendable, so any adversarially donated funds are publicly known to be entirely unspendable.

> SEPA bank transfers do *not* need consent of the receiver! I can send anybody money and they cannot do anything against it.

While it’s technically true that SEPA and similar systems allow pushing funds to an account without the recipient’s explicit consent, this misses the broader point: in traditional finance, bank account information is not the primary interface for interacting with services or transferring funds.

People don’t casually share their IBANs or account numbers for day-to-day financial interaction. Instead, we use controlled instruments like credit/debit cards, and invoicing systems. If you have my debit card number you cannot send funds to my account without my consent, the same is true for the rest of the above.

So while “forced deposits” are technically possible in traditional finance, they’re extremely rare as all interfaces to deposits are heavily regulated, and gated by social, legal, and institutional regulation; this does not hold true for blockchain protocols, which are fully permissionless by default.

More importantly, this type of attack doesn’t even work in TradFi. An OFAC-sanctioned entity cannot wire you money in the first place, as regulated financial institutions block such transfers preemptively. Even in the rare case where tainted funds are sent before sanctions, banks can reclaim or reverse the transaction unilaterally without burdening the innocent recipient.

On-chain, this is impossible. There is no reversal mechanism, no recourse, and no way to reject malicious deposits. No bank there to handle this on your behalf to prevent you from receiving the funds (in a sense that they can actually be spent), no one can prevent an OFAC sanctioned party from sending you funds, and you as a user will have to deal with the cost burden of paying for a transaction to move those funds out of your wallet and even that will not absolve you. 

The proof of this is clear, there has never been a successful instance of a blacklisting attack in tradfi (where stolen / malicious funds were sent to innocent people with the intention of having those people's accounts unbanked and having them blacklisted from financial institutions). 

There have been many successful cases of blacklisting attacks in web3. Tons of innocent users were completely banned from every major off-ramp and centralized exchange during the Tornado Cash "tainting" attacks, and to this day, the majority of these accounts are still marked as illicit by compliance tools like Chainalysis and TRM Labs which prevents these users from interacting with almost any regulated product. 

And again, to reiterate the primary purpose of this CIP has nothing to do with user wallets, it is for smart contracts to be able to sanitize UTxOs. The rest is just a nice side-effect.

When smart contracts were first introduced to Cardano, and the first dApps were being developed the exact approach that you are describing is what they tried. Then they invested a ton of time and money implementing such designs only to realize that these designs fail to scale, in both a literal sense of throughput and ex-units, and in the sense that it becomes entirely impossible to develop and maintain a complex protocol when each and every smart contract in the protocol must manage dozens of different state tokens from different scripts. 

Already there is an absolutely massive amount of security considerations that must be made in the design and development of dApp protocols. Each element of complexity adds up, sure for any individual thing you can say "well why can't the developer just do this and this and this to solve this issue", and you can make the same argument to say that we don't need CIP-112 because everyone can just "use the withdraw zero trick" and "do A and B and C and D to secure it against XYZ attack vectors and in your offchain code do E and F and G to invoke it and query the reward balance to withdraw the correct amount and.." and so forth. Eventually if I spend enough time teaching any bizarre aspect of Cardano development to people, be it the withdraw zero script, or the fact that contracts cannot require witnesses for incoming transfers, or any other number of awful pitfalls and pain-points, they eventually understand and are able to implement the workarounds are write dApps. 

However, inevitably, every single person who reaches this level of understanding of Cardano dApp development, who has developed a smart contract protocol on Cardano that made it to mainnet and has real users, activity, and volume, comes to the exact same conclusion as me. At the very beginning you think "oh, to develop secure feature robust dApps on Cardano all I need is to know about using state tokens, and minting them this way and securing them against smuggling this way, and managing them across multiple contracts this way, and preventing these common attack vectors against state token lifecycle management and these common attack vectors against their minting policies and about the withdraw zero design and these attack vectors against it, and these common pitfalls and these solutions for cyclic dependency issues and if I do all of this then my app is secure and it has all of these features. I know all of this stuff really well so this won't be an issue for me!" Then you realize that every single additional layer of "you have to do this because boilerplate" takes up your capacity reason about your actual protocol, it's logic, and it's attack surfaces. The more you are reasoning about the logic, efficiency, attack surfaces and security of boilerplate, the less you are for your actual protocol. 

We have absolutely ZERO chance at Cardano becoming the best-in-class chain for dApp development if our answer to "how can I make sure the information at my smart contract is trusted" is:

> you have to use a multi-validator Spending / Minting validator, write validation logic to ensure these tokens cannot be smuggled and can be burned in the proper redeemer paths to allow the value to exit the protocol and are minted when users, you must make sure the minting policy allows minting exactly 1 token for each UTxO sent to your script and that the minted token is included in each UTxO sent to the script.

> Oh so if I do all of that THEN the contract can trust the UTxOs at my script?

> No... we haven't even started on the actually implementing the spec of your protocol, all of that is just boilerplate that you need so that you can start actually implementing your protocol. Now you need to actually write the validation logic for what state / value should be present in outputs to your script. 


You are vastly underestimating the constraints of execution budget on the Cardano L1 and the complexity of production smart contract development. The approach you propose, is so inefficient that any dApp that used such contracts would be immediately dead in the market. The throughput of said dApp would be dozens of times lower than a dApp developed with modern smart contract design patterns. Such a dApp would be able to process less than 5 orders against a pool in a given block, meaning for every 5 users you have at a given time, the rest of the users will have a 20 second delay on order fulfillment. If you have 600 active users, that means users will be waiting 40 minutes for their orders to be processed. 

The same thing applies to order books. The amount of orders that a market maker could match in a given transaction would be even worse than an AMM with this design because the order book must burn the state token for each order in a given transaction. 

The example we are discussing, is an extremely simple dApp that has a single contract with fully self-contained state, and even then the complexity is extremely high and it's too inefficient for production. Now consider a complex financial instrument that has 12 different spending validators, each validator has its own state token, and there is an allowed set of transitions between the various spending scripts (inputs from spending script A may produce outputs which go to spending script C or D depending on the redeemer, but never should be able to go to spending script B). Spending script C or D should be able to trust UTxOs that come from spending script A because A has already validated their correctness. So either the state token for script A must now be managed by spending script C or D (and thus minting policy of script A must be invoked along with script C or script D to burn the state token for this UTxO to exit the protocol), or the state token from script A must be burned and script C or D must mint a new state token into a UTxO that is an output from script A conditional on the fact that the token from A has been burned.

I think that the asset-class whitelists for accounts in the Accounts CIP (#1061) can address the problem. This CIP will allow account owners to specify the asset classes in their accounts for which Cardano ledger will keep track of balances and allow direct-deposits/withdrawals. Excluding all other asset classes.

Thus, the high-worth individuals can keep the bulk of their ADA in accounts that are publicly known and immune from receiving meme coins.

This leaves just incoming ADA to worry about in accounts. However, as @HeptaSean mentioned:

> SEPA bank transfers do not need consent of the receiver! I can send anybody money and they cannot do anything against it.

So this problem exists in traditional finance, too, where it is addressed by block-lists and reversing transactions. Block-lists are imperfect because even in tradfi, people can launder money into sybil accounts that bypass the block-lists such that the illicit payment is only detected after the fact. Thus, reversing the transaction is the last line of defense, as @colll78 mentioned:

> (colll78): Even in the rare case where tainted funds are sent before sanctions, banks can reclaim or reverse the transaction unilaterally without burdening the innocent recipient.

Well, we can do the same thing in Cardano:

- if the illicit payment is large enough to cover a tx fee, return to sender (deducting tx fee). This works if the sender's receiving account is known or the payment is large enough to cover minUtxoADA + tx fee.
- if the payment is too small and one-time, then it is insignificant. I would be surprised if most jurisdictions didn't have _de minimis_ rules about the total sum of illicit payments received.
- if there are many tiny payments, return in bulk to sender (if only one sender), pay in bulk as tx fee, or donate to treasury.
    - if there are concerns about the illicit funds entering the treasury, note that it is currently impossible to prevent because the sanctioned entity can just directly donate the funds into treasury or pay them as tx fee. Cardano governance will have to deal with that situation if it arises, possibly surrendering the funds as a treasury withdrawal to the appropriate authorities/victim fund.

High-worth individuals can afford to hire someone or run a bot that will detect and reverse illicit payments in this way.

@nau That is a bad design. There are many reasons why negative numbers are not used in accounting. I also believe that using negative numbers for burning tokens (the opposite of minting) was a bad idea. In this case, if anything, negative value should be used for withdrawals, not deposits. There two more reasons why we should not "abuse" withdrawals field for deposits:
* It would not be backwards compatible. Currently withdrawals use Word64, but in order to introduce sign we would have to change it to Int64, which would prevent the upper half of values from being used any more. I am sure it would not be a deal-breaker, but it is worth mentioning
* More important reason is that we will not want to require a witness for adding funds to the account, for the most part, unless we are to add an optional ability to guard against unauthorized inflow of funds. In either case it would conflict with withdrawals, since we absolutely must require a witness for withdrawals. In other words we do need to distinguish between the two with a different script purpose.

Regarding authentication/thread tokens and managing application state, I'm sympathetic to @colll78's arguments that auth/thread tokens and registry patterns introduce complexity, performance bottlenecks, and cyclic dependencies.

I think that complexity and performance can be mitigated by spending/minting scripts forwarding to CIP-112 transaction-level scripts and by better builtins for onchain queries of auth tokens.

I think that cyclic dependencies are a more general problem for applications that will need to be addressed by a CIP that allows a script address to declare itself as a member of a collection inter-related scripts. As a naive example, instead of using the script hash as the identifier, use a merkle root hash and a path. However, I will concede that the CIP we're presently considering addresses part of the cyclic-dependency problem by avoiding auth tokens and their minting scripts.

A couple of ideas for consideration:

#### Quantifying lost or inactive stake

We are going to gain insight into the scale of the problem after the Midnight glacier drop concludes.  The Night token will be independently valuable and thus it could be reasonably assumed that any Cardano users not claiming their Night tokens either aren't paying attention, don't care, or can't use their keys.  Even though we may not be able to identify which individual addresses represent lost or inactive keys, we will get an idea of that proportion of Ada.

#### Education problem: Staking rewards are not interest but rather reward for active participation

I think it would be good if this CPS attempted to address the education problem regarding why Cardano even has staking.  IE: What is the purpose of staking in the protocol and why do stakers earn rewards for "staking"?

Many users think they are entitled to staking rewards just like receiving interest on a bank account.  A kind of set and forget thing where they just need to do this initial extra step of selecting a stake pool, and now also a DRep, in order to receiving staking rewards.  However, if rewards were supposed to be like interest on a bank account then there would be no need for the selection of a stake pool and the "interest" could simply accumulate automatically.  The code could be simpler too because there would be no need for all this staking stuff.

We need to educate people that staking is voluntary, and those that choose to participate in staking are agreeing to be involved in an active process.  Staking is how the protocol decides which pools get to make blocks, and that underpins the security of the ledger.  Stakers are effectively performing a contract whereby they agree to monitor Cardano network health, and the performance of their chosen pool, in return for receiving a portion of the block production rewards.  Stakers are actually voting for a pool operator using a form of liquid democracy to determine block production and they are expected to change that vote should network conditions change through malicious behaviour or poor performance.  Users that are unable to actually change their chosen pool, should the need arise, are not fulfilling their side of the contract and therefore should not be entitled to rewards.

Lost or inactive stake is not actually contributing to securing Cardano and it would be better if it was somehow "unstaked" for two reasons:
1. It would be better for security since inactive stake provides some older pools with extra control over block production that they shouldn't be entitled to _forever_.  When eventually one of the OG multi-pool operators sells his pool keys to Blackrock then maybe people might understand the security threat from "sticky stake" better.
2. The limited pot of rewards could be directed to the real, active, participants so they receive more instead of throwing rewards away at undeserving wallets.

#### Ways to mitigate the problem

One possible mitigation strategy could be to automatically deem stake no-longer active after say 1yr, thus requiring re-staking or at least confirmation of current stake pool selection.  A kind of proof-of-life that the user is capable of signing with his keys.  This would at least place a limit on pools continuing to accumulate "sticky" or inactive stake.

Exposing the integer balance directly to phase-2 scripts would break determinism because it's global state that can be changed independently from the transaction you're looking at.

Determinism for phase-2 scripts is important because phase-2 is expensive and you only want to run it once. If we lose determinism, then every node in the network will constantly have to re-evaluate phase-2 for every transaction, every time it learns about a new block.

@michele-nuzzi 
For clarity, let's review how time-validity intervals work:

- The transaction creator can optionally attach an interval restricting the slots at which the transaction can be included in a block. If such an interval is not included, the transaction can be included in blocks at any slots.
- Phase 1 checks that the current slot is within the transaction's interval.
- Phase 2 does not see the current slot, but it sees the time-validity interval. Thus, onchain scripts must assume that the transaction might be evaluated in any slot within the interval, and can only apply assertions to the interval bounds themselves.

The proposed mechanism for account balances will do the same thing, but for every asset class for which the account tracks a balance:

- The transaction submitter can optionally attach an interval restricting the balance of an asset at the account.
- Phase 1 ensures that the account is initialized to track a balance for that asset and that the balance falls within that interval.
- Phase 2 does not see the actual balance, but it can see the balance interval. Onchain scripts must assume that the balance falls within the interval, and they can only apply assertions to the interval bounds.

The main different is that we allow up to one balance interval to be defined per asset class tracked by an account.

Thanks for the feedback. I've addressed them via the last 2 commits,  let me clarify my approach and the reasoning behind it:

### What I modified

* **Abstract and Motivation**: I rewrote these sections explicitly for the broader community. They now provide all the context needed to understand what the proposal does and why it matters, without requiring readers to parse the technical details. This ensures accessibility for non-specialists.
* **Minor edits**:

  * Consistently renaming “Φalanx” to “Phalanx” for clarity and readability.
  * Fixing typos and small grammar issues (for example, “serie” to “series,” “nocne” to “nonce”).
  * Standardizing notation and symbols (for example, replacing inconsistent η/φ stream labels, subscript formatting, LaTeX expressions).
  * Harmonizing section titles and headers (ensuring consistency between the ToC and the body text).
  * Correcting anchor links and dummy numbering inconsistencies in the Table of Contents.
  * Improving readability of formulas and diagrams with clearer formatting.
  * Adding a copyright note clarifying the limited role of AI tools (copy-editing, formatting) while affirming that all technical content is original human work.

### What I did not modify

* **Specification**: I deliberately did not touch this section. By design, it is the normative reference for implementors. It must remain detailed and rigorous so that an implementation can be performed solely from this section. Diluting it for accessibility would undermine interoperability and leave implementors without a precise blueprint. The CIP template itself makes this explicit: *“The technical specification should describe the proposed improvement in sufficient technical detail… enough information that an implementation can be performed solely on the basis of the design in the CIP.”*
* **Rationale**: Also untouched. It is a **technical justification for experts** (cryptographers, researchers, engineers). In this section, we explain for example:

  * why we ended up with a VDF instead of another primitive,
  * why the design raises the cost of grinding,
  * why it reduces settlement times,
  * and why we recommend the chosen parameters.
    These explanations are essential for expert review and for future teams who will take this work forward.
* **Numbering**: I did not remove numbering. This is part of the semantic structure of a **highly structured and complex proposal**. Numbering is essential for navigation, clarity, and precision in referencing specific parts of the design. Removing it would weaken the document. Moreover, this feedback is not part of the official [CIP-0001 guidelines](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0001). Addressing the arguments 1 by 1 raised upstream in this PR  against numbering:
    1. **Convention**: It was noted that most other CIPs do not use numbering. This is because most of them are much smaller in scope. For short proposals, numbering may not be needed. For larger, highly technical ones like this, numbering is in fact the convention since it is the only way to maintain structure and readability.
    2. **Editing burden**: It was suggested that numbering could be “fastidious” for future editors to maintain. This perspective is misleading. From the editor’s side it may look like overhead, but from the author’s side, writing such a complex document without numbering is essentially impossible. Numbering is what allows the writer and later reviewers to navigate and reference specific sections consistently.
    3. **Technical claim**: It was argued that numbering creates technical issues. In practice, the opposite is true: numbering adds semantic precision. Removing it degrades clarity, and since GitHub already adds dummy numbering when anchors collide, stripping explicit numbering makes the document more confusing, not less.

### Conclusion

The CIP framework already provides the right balance:

* **Abstract and Motivation**: Accessibility for the community.
* **Specification**: Rigorous blueprint for implementors.
* **Rationale**: Expert justification for why the design is sound and why we made these choices.

Removing numbering or reducing the technical depth of the Specification or Rationale undermines their purpose. If the CIP asks for a Specification, then it must be allowed to appear in its proper form, with full rigor and structure.

Equally, CIP-0001 does not require that the Specification or Rationale be “optimized” for a broader audience, nor does it introduce the idea of “complexity boundaries.” Since this concept is subjective and reader-dependent, it seems more practical to ensure accessibility through the Abstract and Motivation, while keeping the Specification and Rationale focused on their expert audience. 

Appendices may be useful for secondary or supporting material, but in this document all content is referenced and integral, nothing here is secondary. 

We would therefore prefer that this proposal not be influenced by ongoing experiments or debates on alternative structures, as it already complies with the current guidelines. In addition, the document has been carefully written and reviewed by peer experts to ensure internal consistency and correctness.

> In other words, the only time when it can be visible whether an SPO or DRep is malicious is from the actions they perform. For example if a block producer is intentionally trying to fork the network.

Totally agree, there is no transparency and nobody can tell how a pool operator or DRep will act in the future.  The Ouroboros protocol assumes that people can and will re-stake.  But lost / inactive stake won't and this stake provides extra voting / block production power.

How much does it cost to purchase voting / block production power?  If I buy Ada then we know how much that costs, but I will be able to buy that voting / block production power more cheaply by buying some DRep / pool keys that have a lot of lost / inactive stake _permanently_ "attached" to them.

There are two issues:
1. Obviously there is the security concern I am articulating.  We can debate how significant this is currently because we have no way of really knowing how much lost / inactive stake there really is.  But we do know that it will accumulate over time.
2. However there is also an unfair competitive advantage concern which can be compounded over time.  This is because OG pool operators have an unfair competitive advantage whereby they can create new pools charging lower costs and increase the costs on their old pool as a way to cross subsidise expenses.  They know the lost / inactive stake in their old pool can't / won't move.  This allows them to accumulate more stake in their new pools by undercutting competitors whilst still retaining the lost / inactive stake in their old pool.  Then rinse and repeat over time.  Lost / inactive stake will accumulate in all pools over time but arguably more in lower cost pools or ones that get high wallet rankings since time poor people are probably both more likely to simply click the highest ranked pool and also to lose their keys.

    So how do you get a high wallet ranking?  Well one way is to be cheap but another way is by having high pledge.  And, this lost / inactive stake also allows the OG operator to shift his pledge with less backlash from stakers.  This is because the lost / inactive stake isn't watching and doesn't care, but more pledge will attract new stakers to his new low cost pool.

    Now this leads back to the security issue as they accumulate lost / inactive stake over time _especially_ since we don't actually know whether a new low cost pool is actually run by an OG operator with other pools benefiting from lost / inactive stake.  Any OG operator can create any number of new pools and it is really impossible for the community to know who is actually pulling the strings behind the scenes.

The set and forget mechanism with no expiry that Cardano currently uses for staking to pools or DReps is flawed.

> In my opinion it is a lot more dangerous for a whole lot of stake to get undelegated at once, when all of the ADA that was lost over many years gets removed from block production.

I think that depends on assumptions about who is pulling the strings on the pool / DRep keys benefiting from the increased block production / voting power that lost Ada provides.

I have a few thoughts that make me hesitant about this CIP:

Cardano's Proof-of-Stake launch was *extremely hyped up*. A lot of people had joined the community during that hype and staked their ADA then. Fast-forward to now, there is a lull from Cardano's disappointing DeFi applications. I think it is a sure bet that most people are not paying attention right now. If we implemented expirations during this lull period, I highly doubt the total delegated stake would recover post-expiration. We could see our stake participation drop from 70% to 40% or less.

> In Cardano, **staking is voluntary and active**.

This is not accurate. Passive vs active depends on how frequently actions need to be taken. If I only need to adjust my delegation once every few years, how is that active? If my pool is doing fine and acting honestly, I may never need to change my delegation in my lifetime. *PoS is designed to be passive when times are good*. It is like voting participation: most people only vote during troubled times.

---
> ... accrued rewards for inactive accounts would go into treasury, instead of being added to the account. This would solve the exponential run-off without sacrificing the stability and security of the system. Also, from the perspective of the account owner it would be equivalent to "Expired delegations simply stop earning and can be renewed at any time."

Given my above thoughts, @lehins approach is the only one that seems safe because:
1. It won't cause a significant drop in Cardano's total stake due to Cardano's popularity currently being at a low.
2. It won't punish rational actors who are *correctly* behaving passively in a PoS system.

> I think it is a sure bet that most people are not paying attention right now. If we implemented expirations during this lull period, I highly doubt the total delegated stake would recover post-expiration. We could see our stake participation drop from 70% to 40% or less.

This is why we combined the expirations with the second part of the CIP that includes a change to distribute the full rewards pot.  It is a counter-balancing mechanism to mitigate this concern because with the change, the lower the stake participation gets, the higher the reward for staking.  This is easiest to see in our [tool](https://spo-incentives.vercel.app/) by experimenting with the `Staked Ratio` slider with rewards mode set to `Current` and `Full`.  The latter represents the change suggested by this CIP.

Unfortunately if we simply returned excess rewards from inactive accounts to the treasury, it would defeat this purpose because now there would be no counter-balancing mechanism to offset a worrisome drop in stake participation.

> Passive vs active depends on how frequently actions need to be taken. If I only need to adjust my delegation once every few years, how is that active? If my pool is doing fine and acting honestly, I may never need to change my delegation in my lifetime. PoS is designed to be passive when times are good. It is like voting participation: most people only vote during troubled times.

The **initial** act of delegating is active because it requires a delegator to select a pool and then submit a transaction.  From that point on, it requires regular re-assessment *somehow* to actually know whether or not your pool is doing fine and acting honestly (this is also technically active, though it isn't necessary reflected on-chain).  As it stands right now we have no way of knowing if users are doing that re-assessment and so they could be empowering malicious behaviors unintentionally.  Especially if those users *can't* move their delegation due to lost keys, death, etc.

This CIP's intention is to increase the *quality* of delegated stake (as @WhatisRT mentioned) by adding a mechanism to enforce that periodic re-assessment AND by rewarding such activity more directly.

There is also the issue of reserve sustainability to consider (This relates to full-pot distribution. The second point of this CIP)

Yesterday the Leios CIP was published.  The specific area to draw your attention to is the charts under [Operating Costs](https://github.com/cardano-scaling/CIPs/blob/leios/CIP-%3F%3F%3F%3F/README.md#operating-costs).

Consider that in order to match our rewards rate by 2030 we'd need to sustain 41.9 TPS worth of transactions (actual transactions, not capacity).  If I'm understanding their wording correctly, they are also suggesting that it may be 5x that amount (209.5 TPS) because SPOs don't receive 100% of rewards, it's actually closer to 20% (I believe this is an average of pool margin, fixed fee, etc. but it's not quite clear what they mean).  Furthermore, in [CPS-22](https://github.com/Cerkoryn/CIPs/blob/sticky-stake/CPS-0022/README.md) we projected that the rewards APY is on track to be 0.6% by 2030.

I do not believe this is sustainable, and yet it is a hard problem to solve.  Simply adding partner chain AVS (or other rewards income) *WITHOUT* adding some sort of proof-of-life mechanism amplifies the compounding rewards problem and is also unlikely to be enough.  This CIP enhances sustainability by being slightly more selective about which wallets are eligible for rewards (i.e., active once every `delegationLifetime` epochs) therefore allowing us to stretch out our reserves even more.

> This is why we combined the expirations with the second part of the CIP ... the lower the stake participation gets, the higher the reward for staking.

IMHO higher rewards is not going to meaningfully influence the total stake delegated right now. If everyone agreed that ADA was valuable, then offering them more ADA *would* incentivize action. But what if they don't value ADA? This is offering them more of an asset they don't care about. People are currently leaving the Cardano community because they don't see value in it anymore. The inactive stake is likely from this latter group which means offering slightly higher rewards is not going to work. The incentives are targeting the wrong group of people. The current inactive stake will only become active again if they actually see value in Cardano. It is sad to say, but I think there is a decent percentage of Cardano's security that is being propped up by users who have just "written-off" their ADA. (I'm open to data that proves this wrong.)

That being said, if the confiscated rewards from inactive delegators could go to the active delegators, I think that would be ideal. But I don't know how complicated that calculation would be for the ledger. My biggest concern is that we don't touch the total stake delegated for now.

> There is also the issue of reserve sustainability to consider ...

This CIP doesn't really address this, especially if we just confiscate the rewards from inactive delegators and pay them out to active delegators. The same amount of the reserves are being spent. We could recycle the confiscated rewards back into the reserve, but then we aren't rewarding active delegators.

IMHO both the inactive stake and the sustainability issue are solved by making Cardano actually useful to the world. If its DeFi was actually useful, its tx volume (and collected fees) would increase and so would the value of ADA vs fiat. Right now, Cardano blocks seem to average about [90% empty](https://cexplorer.io/block) so increasing TPS to 50 won't do anything.

> The current inactive stake will only become active again if they actually see value in Cardano. I agree, but "Increasing the value of Cardano" is a much broader and harder problem to solve. This CIP is much more narrowly-scoped. > It is sad to say, but I think there is a decent percentage of Cardano's security that is being propped up by users who have just "written-off" their ADA. (I'm open to data that proves this wrong.) This is good from the perspective of an EXTERNAL attacker, but bad from the perspective of an INSIDER threat who might already be accumulating lots of stake (or purchasing an established pool with it) with malicious intent. > That being said, if the confiscated rewards from inactive delegators could go to the active delegators, I think that would be ideal. But I don't know how complicated that calculation would be for the ledger. That's exactly what this CIP is aiming to achieve and I think it is arguably simpler than how the rewards are currently distributed. Right now, the rewards pot is built based on TOTAL circulating ADA, but then only the ACTIVE-staked proportion is distributed, with the remaining going back to the reserves. The CIP simplifies that to simply distribute the entire proportion to active, eligible stakers. I haven't been able to find any good documentation on this other then section 5.5.1 of the Shelley Delegation spec: However (as explained in the CIP) I think the censorship issue they describe there is no longer relevant. > This CIP doesn't really address this, especially if we just confiscate the rewards from inactive delegators and pay them out to active delegators. The same amount of the reserves are being spent. We could recycle the confiscated rewards back into the reserve, but then we aren't rewarding active delegators. The CIP touches on this in the Rationale under the section `Option to adjust Rho`. However, we are *already* returning excess rewards to the reserves. What we are suggesting is that we instead distribute that excess to active delegators, and then we could lower Rho accordingly.

No, HFs are triggered by the ratification of a governance action now, and this depends entirely on the ledger state at the epoch boundary. There is no need to revisit and HFC compatibility since none of the timings change.

If we are going to highlight a supposed security concern related to deregistering a small fraction of the currently staked Ada then it is only fair to also highlight the security concern that arises from _not_ deregistering this Ada.

The voting rights, or block production rights, for this inactive / inaccessible Ada can currently be purchased at a substantial discount to the Ada price by purchasing the pool keys or DRep keys to which this Ada is permanently attached.

In the case of a stake pool, the current operator can simply register new pools and encourage active participants to move to his new pools.  The inactive stake will stay in the old pool and he can sell these old pool keys to the malicious adversary.  Let's say his old pool has 5M Ada of inactive stake.  To a well intentioned pool operator this inactive stake is currently worth maybe 5% of 2.5% per year income (if pool fees are levied at 5%).  This equates to around 6,250 Ada per year in revenue, reducing over time.  An adversary might be able to purchase these pool keys for something like this amount up front, or maybe more, or maybe less, depending on the operator.  However there is no way that the cost of these pool keys in the hands of a rational willing seller will be anything close to the full cost of the 5M Ada.  The most that anyone can earn in staking rewards from this 5M inactive stake is currently 125,000 Ada per year if pool fees were increased to 100%.  However, these keys still provide the adversary with the full 5M worth of block production consensus power and since the adversary is interested in doing adverse things this is what he cares about.  Consequently he can purchase 5M worth of consensus power for _much less_ than 5M Ada and he knows this 5M Ada will always back his malicious activity because it is inactive and can't move _forever_.

Due to the fact that nobody can really know who is actually running a pool, there is no way that anyone can even know if an adversary hasn't already accumulated significant portions of inactive staked Ada by purchasing other pool keys.

An adversary could already be controlling significant portions of all the inactive stake.

Hi, I think I've got the new Leios intuition; can you sanity-check this?

Today we run Praos under a Δ-synchronous model: blocks need to diffuse within Δ. That constrains how far we can push block size and Plutus budget because larger blocks and budgets stress propagation relative to Δ.

In this Leios version, a block additionally commits (succinctly) to extra transaction work that is endorsed/validated off this critical constrained propagation path. The commitment is small enough to keep block propagation within Δ, so Praos base safety/liveness is preserved. Meanwhile, during the time the block diffuses, the network tries to finalize the extra work via endorsements in the next block, again keeping this certificate small enough to keep block propagation within Δ. When that succeeds, we raise the effective throughput of one block without lengthening the critical path.

Whether the extra work finalizes in time (in the next block) depends on network conditions—latency, bandwidth, peer degree/topology, and adversarial load—not just node hardware. The nice part is that this Leios exposes parameters (e.g., EB size/rate or endorsement windows) that can be tuned empirically and, if desired, dynamically, so we can track headroom as conditions of our network topology and capacity change over time.
