Edit: Having thought about it a little and done some experiments, there's two comments I want to add in response.

The claim that "under strict evaluation, intermediates get consumed and freed right away" _may_ be theoretically true, but this is definitely not how the SECP machine that evaluates UPLC works. To illustrate, I've put together a simple set of benchmarks comparing a 'fused' implementation of `zip3` to one based on two calls to `zip2`. I used Plutarch as the implementation language, but this should translate to Plinth or Aiken just as well:

```haskell
module Main (main) where

import PlutusCore (Contains, DefaultUni)
import Data.Kind (Type)
import Plutarch.Prelude (Term, S, PBuiltinList (PNil, PCons), 
  PInteger, pconstant, (#), (:-->), 
  phoistAcyclic, plam, (#*), (#+), pfix, pmatch, PlutusRepr, 
  pcon, (#$), ppairDataBuiltin, pdata, PIsData, pfromData,
  PBuiltinPair (PBuiltinPair))
import Test.Tasty (testGroup)
import Plutarch.Test.Bench (
  bench,
  defaultMain,
 )
import Plutarch.Test.Utils (precompileTerm)

main :: IO ()
main = defaultMain $ testGroup "Zip" [
  testGroup "pzip3Direct" [
    bench "length 5" (precompileTerm (pzip3Direct f) # plistA5 # plistB5 # plistC5),
    bench "length 10" (precompileTerm (pzip3Direct f) # plistA10 # plistB10 # plistC10),
    bench "length 15" (precompileTerm (pzip3Direct f) # plistA15 # plistB15 # plistC15)
    ],
  testGroup "pzip3Indirect" [
    bench "length 5" (precompileTerm (pzip3Indirect f) # plistA5 # plistB5 # plistC5),
    bench "length 10" (precompileTerm (pzip3Indirect f) # plistA10 # plistB10 # plistC10),
    bench "length 15" (precompileTerm (pzip3Indirect f) # plistA15 # plistB15 # plistC15)
    ]
  ]

-- Test data

plistA5 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistA5 = pconstant (iota 1 5)

plistA10 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistA10 = pconstant (iota 1 10)

plistA15 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistA15 = pconstant (iota 1 15)

plistB5 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistB5 = pconstant (iota 6 10)

plistB10 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistB10 = pconstant (iota 6 15)

plistB15 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistB15 = pconstant (iota 6 20)

plistC5 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistC5 = pconstant (iota 21 25)

plistC10 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistC10 = pconstant (iota 21 30)

plistC15 :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PBuiltinList PInteger)
plistC15 = pconstant (iota 21 35)

f :: forall (s :: S) . Term s (PInteger :--> PInteger :--> PInteger :--> PInteger)
f = phoistAcyclic $ plam $ \x y z -> x #* (y #+ z)

pzip3Direct :: forall (a :: S -> Type) (b :: S -> Type) (c :: S -> Type) (d :: S -> Type) (s :: S) .
  (DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr a,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr b,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr c,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr d) =>
  Term s (a :--> b :--> c :--> d) -> 
  Term s (PBuiltinList a :--> PBuiltinList b :--> PBuiltinList c :--> PBuiltinList d)
pzip3Direct g = pfix $ \self -> plam $ \xs ys zs -> pmatch xs $ \case
  PNil -> pcon PNil
  PCons x xs' -> pmatch ys $ \case
    PNil -> pcon PNil
    PCons y ys' -> pmatch zs $ \case
      PNil -> pcon PNil
      PCons z zs' -> pcon . PCons (g # x # y # z) $ self # xs' # ys' # zs'

pzip3Indirect :: forall (a :: S -> Type) (b :: S -> Type) (c :: S -> Type) (d :: S -> Type) (s :: S) .
  (DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr a,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr b,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr c,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr d,
    PIsData b,
    PIsData c) =>
  Term s (a :--> b :--> c :--> d) -> 
  Term s (PBuiltinList a :--> PBuiltinList b :--> PBuiltinList c :--> PBuiltinList d)
pzip3Indirect g = plam $ \xs ys zs -> 
  pzip2 (plam $ \x yz -> pmatch yz $ \case
    PBuiltinPair y z -> g # x # pfromData y # pfromData z) # xs #$ pzip2 (plam $ \y z -> ppairDataBuiltin # pdata y # pdata z) # ys # zs

-- Helpers

iota :: Integer -> Integer -> [Integer]
iota start stop = [start, start + 1 .. stop]

pzip2 :: forall (a :: S -> Type) (b :: S -> Type) (c :: S -> Type) (s :: S) . 
  (DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr a,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr b,
    DefaultUni `Contains` PlutusRepr c) => 
  Term s (a :--> b :--> c) -> 
  Term s (PBuiltinList a :--> PBuiltinList b :--> PBuiltinList c)
pzip2 g = pfix $ \self -> plam $ \xs ys -> pmatch xs $ \case
  PNil -> pcon PNil
  PCons x xs' -> pmatch ys $ \case
    PNil -> pcon PNil
    PCons y ys' -> pcon . PCons (g # x # y) $ self # xs' # ys'
```

Overall, the proposal is sensible. @zliu41 has performed preliminary experiments where applying `Force` to `Delay` stores the result, so that it is computed at most once. It turns out to be not vastly more expensive (and, of course, sometimes far less expensive) than when applying `Force` to `Delay` recomputes each time.

Terminology: The proposal uses "true laziness" to refer to the case where applying `Force` to `Delay` computes at most once, as opposed to the version that recomputes every time. Better to use the standard terminology from the literature: *call-by-need* -- compute at most once and store the result; *call-by-name* -- recompute every time. The term "lazy" is a synonym for call-by-need. Haskell is call-by-need or lazy (no need to say "true lazy") while Force-Delay in Plutus is call-by-name (not lazy, or even "false lazy").
@wadler - agreed, better to use the standard terminology. Will change.

[lazy-delay-force.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26065364/lazy-delay-force.pdf)

The summary of my evaluation is attached. TLDR: lazy delay/force is about 2x the cost of by-name delay/force. For well-optimized programs that don't have excessive unnecessary delay/force, the overhead is less than 3%. For poorly-optimized programs, the overhead can be about 10%, or even 90%+ in extreme cases.

Incidentally I find the motivation a bit weak, as I couldn't think of a good example where laziness is a clear win. I'll look into and try to understand the Boehm-Berrarducci use case.

The attack (turning a non-programmable token into a programmable one) will be impossible after the fix. The fix would enforce that:
Any token minted through the issuance minting policy must either already be a registered programmable token or must be registered as a programmable token in the transaction in which the minting occurs. The problem with the current approach is that you can mint a token with the issuance minting policy **without registering it in the programmable token directory as a programmable token**, the token will be minted and included in some output to `programmableLogicBase` and because it is not yet registered as a programmable token, that UTxO can be spent from `programmableLogicBase` to any address outside of the programmable tokens mini-ledger (ie. my wallet address). Wallets will not mark this as a programmable token because it is not registered as a programmable token on the programmable token directory, indeed at that point in time the token would **NOT** be a programmable token because it can exit the mini-ledger freely and is not subjected to any programmable logic within the mini-ledger. During this time, wallets would include this token in other UTxOs with other programmable / non-programmable assets under the expectation that this token will always be a non-programmable asset. After this token has circulated and is present in UTxOs both inside and outside the programmable tokens mini-ledger, the attacker could register it as a programmable token at which point all the UTxOs with this token in the mini-ledger are subjected to its logic and thus bricked. 

The key invariant this vulnerability breaks is that ***programmable tokens can never exist outside the mini-ledger***, the problem is that you can mint a non-programmable token from the issuance policy, and then at your own convenience, register that token as a programmable token and brick any DEX pools / user UTxOs in the mini-ledger with that token.

>What's the benefit of this? Would it fix any issues or is it a performance improvement? At this level of optimisation, I believe optimisation is possible but in the thousands of lovelaces, at the cost of a more complex and hence error prone redeemer.

The main goal of script optimization is not to reduce transaction fees (although that is a meaningful byproduct), it's primarily to increase dApp throughput, and secondarily to expand the range of what features are possible and feasible to implement within dApps. This is critical for any production dApp which expects non-trivial onchain activity, which is why you see protocols like Minswap, SundaeSwap, Liqwid, and others that need to be able to facilitate more than a handful of concurrent users spend so much time and effort on micro-optimization. If a DEX processing contract hits the transaction ex-unit limits with 16 orders then the dApps throughput is less than 1 request / second, and with backlog users can end up waiting close to half an hour for their orders to process. All production dApps fall into one of two categories with respect to how they handle this:
1. Dedicate significant effort into optimizing the ex-unit consumption of their contracts. Micro-optimizations, indexing, taking advantage of ledger invariants, witness-driven-complexity-collapse and all the other modern design patterns. 
2. Minimize onchain logic and move trust assumptions offchain (ex. the authority to process orders is limited to an admin key and as such the validators can afford to omit expensive validation logic by relying on the administrative authority to act honestly with respect to the components that aren't directly enforced on-chain)

The theoretical throughput limitations for most dApps right now are between 40-50 orders per block, this is around the threshold at which you have enough capacity to support most onchain activity right now and you only really see this threshold exceeded and the subsequent throttling become a UX issue for short bursts during very high interest launches or liquidation events; but for most onchain activity now, the current level of optimization in these dApps is sufficient. 

The problem is that with programmable tokens they won't be able to achieve anywhere near that level of throughput because a huge percentage of the transaction ex-budget will be consumed by the core mini-ledger contracts, and the individual programmable token transfer logic contracts. For a programmableToken/Ada pool, without even considering the ex-unit costs of the token's transferLogicScript, you hit the ex-unit limit far before processing even 15 swaps in a block. At this point any non-trivial user activity hits this threshold and UX slows to a crawl. Ex-units are already a huge constraint for throughput and feature capabilities of dApps today, this issue becomes even more prominent for dApps on the programmable tokens mini-ledger since a huge portion of the budget is already consumed by the mini-ledger smart contracts which are entirely out of their control. If the ex-unit footprint of the mini-ledger isn't minimized to the absolute limit then programmable token dApps will be forced to gut logic or leave end users to suffer the UX downgrade of request bottlenecks. 

Also transaction fees aren't the only fees that are impacted by throughput, dApp infrastructure costs are directly correlated to the amount of batches that must be processed, if 60 swap requests can be processed in a single batch, this results in substantially less work (especially with respect to coordination) for batchers than processing three batches of 20 swaps, and this difference can be reflected in the batcher fee.  

We aren't talking about micro-optimizations; we are talking about an average difference in efficiency of 30-80% across every class of real-world use-cases.

#### **The Challenge Window ($X$ Epochs)**
A **Constitutionality Challenge** can only be triggered during the first $X$ epochs of a Governance Action’s lifetime. 
* **Inside the Window:** If a CC member votes `No`, the "Optimistic" presumption is voided. The action immediately transitions to **Challenged** status.

To really simplify this proposal, it essentially changes how the ledger treats non-voting CC members on active governance actions.

Instead of treating non-voting from CC members as a NO, this change defaults the CC to a YES, as long as no CC member actively casts a NO vote. If even one NO vote is cast, the ledger reverts to the current rules, where not voting is treated as a NO.

I see two main risks:

1. Governance Action proposers could submit GAs close to the end of an epoch and collude with DReps to push a change through before any CC member notices it.
2. CC members hold an ultimate veto and could abuse their power by casting a NO vote right before an action would be approved. For example, let's assume a parameter change only obtains the necessary DRep or SPO votes in the last epoch of its lifetime. Because no CC member has voted yet, everyone assumes the action will pass. Then, in the final slots of the epoch, a single CC member votes NO to effectively veto the action, since the other CC members cannot quickly enough cast their YES votes. (Shout out to Megan for highlighting this!)

These are the main attack vectors I currently see.

> That goes against the whole principle of the state-agency / typed protocols scheme I'm afraid.

The protocol is still typed and can still be usefully formalised, but yes, modelling the real behaviour does require mixed choice, which is not currently available in the machinery used in the Haskell implementation. This is semantically already true of the existing protocols, where in StCanAwait of chain sync the initiator may send RequestNext even though it has “no agency” — this is what you call pipelining, but since all “sessions” share the same communication channel without tagging their messages, I think it is fair to consider those pipelining instances just a matter of perspective, like the choice of gauge in quantum field theory.

What I’d like to achieve here is that we define a useful network protocol befitting the Leios information flow requirements, not moulded to or limited by the existing code structure of other mini-protocols in a particular Cardano node implementation.

It is also quite easy to conform to my proposed protocol using the existing Haskell machinery by applying the pipelining approach to run a number of instances of the protocol with a fixed choice of N (e.g. N=1 to get normal request–response). This requires slightly more resources within the node but saves complexity cost in the Haskell codebase by reusing existing infrastructure.

> …, and for votes the responses can carry multiple anyway.

My proposal changes the MsgLeiosVote to carry exactly one vote because then the message has a predictable cost. Allowing a list of votes within a single message means that the responder can cause unpredictable resource usage — in my proposal an initiator may ask for 1000 votes after which it expects to receive no more than 1000 votes (until it asks for more later).

---

I appreciate that this deviates from the trodden path in Cardano, and I’d like to ask you to consider this with an open mind given that Reactive Streams have been around for more than a decade in the JDK, meaning that this communication principle is well proven.

Just wanted to leave a short comment here to share the relevance to the Cardano IBC Incubator project, as the incubator was mentioned several times in the initial CPS and following conversations, so I just want to clarify the practical implications for us:

Roughly that project is about restoring Cosmos-native cryptographic artifacts on Cardano. To keep the scope of discussion narrow, two important things that includes are Merkleized chain state roots in block headers, but also that block finality/consensus is directly linked to a validator voting mechanism, so once a block is committed, it can't be reversed, so when a header gets produced you can be safe under the assumption of this being the canonical chain tip. Two counterparty chains can very safely just keep exchanging headers and know very quickly and trustlessly what is happening on the other chain, as a factor not just of the merkle root but also finality dynamics.

We have a highly engineered solution for this in our Cardano implementation which I won't dig too deep into, but importantly, for this upgrade to be of use in this type of project, we still have the same finality issue. That is, in the longterm, I'm not sure if this upgrade independently unlocks any big doors in blockchain interop without improvements to finality, though it may have been framed that way earlier.

You can already establish a trusted Merkle root over a subset of UTxOs that your application cares about, especially clean to do this with an STT pattern. That is, developers can already construct on-chain Merkle roots for subsets of the ledger that they care about, which is what we've done for the incubator, but we can't "fake" finality over that same subset in the same way, so in practical terms this CIP-0178 upgrade wouldn't necessarily be covering any major pain point in the incubator project on its own.

The problem is that for multi-chain interoperability light IBC, you need lightweight state proofs that can be verified onchain, and the only state proof that Cardano has access to that can be feasibly verified onchain are mithril proofs. Mithril proofs attest to the block-header, so in Ethereum you can use them to prove that a given Cardano block-header is authentic (its authenticity is attested to by the mithril stake-weighted attestation). The problem is that as it stands now you cannot actually do anything useful with this certified block-header because it is impossible to prove anything about the transactions within the block that the block_header corresponds to. 

So, the current flow would be:
1, A Cardano block is produced `block_header_a`
2. At some point after, Mithril signers produce a stake-weighted commitment which attests to the authenticity of `block_header_a`, we call this `block_header_a_attestation`
3.  `block_header_a` and `block_header_a_attestation` are provided as inputs to an Ethereum smart contract, and the smart contract verifies the mithril attestation `block_header_a_attestation` at which point it knows that `block_header_a` is indeed a valid Cardano block. 
4. Now that we know that `block_header_a` is an authentic block, want to prove, on Ethereum, that some Cardano transaction happened in the block corresponding to `block_header_a`, the `block_header_a` has the `block_hash` which is the hash of the raw cbor of the block which contains the transactions, so to validate anything about the transactions that happened in that block we need to pass the preimage of that block hash (the actual block cbor) to the Ethereum validator validate it and then extract the relevant transactions from that cbor and validate them. The problem is that blocks can be 80kb+ when you consider the need to manipulate / deserialize the cbor in the consuming contract (ie. Ethereum) and this is completely infeasible within gas limits of the vast majority of chains (Ethereum, Solana, and every other major chain).

@zliu41 - it isn't clear how to do this in general. Let me give an example in context to illustrate why this is so difficult.

As part of current work on the [Grumplestiltskin project](https://github.com/mlabs-haskell/grumplestiltskin/tree/koz/direct-ec), we have been considering elliptic curves over second-degree finite field extensions. These are even worse than the example given, as second-degree field extensions are pairs of finite field elements, which makes their operations (particularly multiplication and division) far more involved. In particular, they require yet more 'auxiliary values' (specifically a field irreducible), and each operation in particular corresponds to quite a large number of builtins. 

As part of our work, we did a pedantic comparison of both direct and indirect representations, even given the issues described already. We have found that [indirect representations are significantly better](https://github.com/mlabs-haskell/grumplestiltskin/blob/koz/direct-ec/goldens/extension-ec.bench.golden#L2-L5), but still have huge costs, caused by the precise problem I described before.

As to why this is hard to avoid, consider the case of [elliptic curve point scaling](https://github.com/mlabs-haskell/grumplestiltskin/blob/koz/direct-ec/src/Grumplestiltskin/Degree2/EllipticCurveID.hs#L121-L145). If we observe the implementation, we can see that the `t` argument (the point being scaled) is re-used every time our [exponentiation-by-squaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation_by_squaring) encounters an odd exponent in the 'ladder', which in bad cases can be as frequently as `log(n)`, where `n` is the scalar's value. This is done by 'calling out' to elliptic curve point addition, which has to happen, as one argument is unknown (and may easily be the point at infinity). How we would avoid repeated re-evaluation of the `t` argument in this context is not clear to me: you can't 'float out' the evaluation of the `k1` continuation, as it must be used as a 'component' of the _new_ continuation produced as a result of `doubled #+ t'`.

Now, I might be wrong in this _particular_ case, and it could be possible to avoid this. However, I certainly can't think of how. Furthermore, this is a case that's both extremely natural in this situation, and likely to be extremely bad. If you see [the scaling benchmarks](https://github.com/mlabs-haskell/grumplestiltskin/blob/koz/direct-ec/goldens/extension-ec.bench.golden#L18-L21), you can observe that the exunit and memory cost flies off the handle pretty quickly. Furthermore, the exponent in this context is tiny (64), whereas in [practice](https://github.com/mlabs-haskell/grumplestiltskin/blob/sean/debug-test-failure/src/Grumplestiltskin/Verify.hs), the required scalar will be a high-entropy random number which is far, _far_ bigger. And this is just for _verification_ - constructing the necessary bilinear pairing function would be many, _many_ times worse than this.

@lehins If I understand correctly, in your proposed scenario with an NCL parameter (or similar check), the validation only occurs when a treasury withdrawal Governance Action (GA) is submitted. At that exact moment, the system verifies how many lovelaces have already flowed out of the treasury during the defined NCL term.

The flaw in this approach is that it fails to account for active, pending treasury withdrawals that are live but haven't been enacted yet.

Because the system only checks against enacted withdrawals at the time of submission, we could accidentally exceed the NCL limit if multiple pending GAs are eventually approved.

Here is how that could happen:

- The Limit: The NCL is set to 300M ADA, and 250M ADA has already been withdrawn.

- The Pending Actions: Two new treasury withdrawals are live, requesting 25M ADA each. If both pass, we hit our exact maximum of 300M ADA.

- The Loophole: While those two are still pending, someone submits a third withdrawal for 10M ADA. Because the first two haven't been enacted yet, the system only sees the initial 250M ADA spent. The 10M ADA transaction passes the submission check.

- The Result: If all three are approved by voters, 310M ADA is withdrawn, breaking the NCL.

Despite this edge case, I still believe we should implement the NCL check. We can reasonably rely on the "social layer" of Cardano governance to identify this overlapping overspend and vote down the excess requests. Once the pending GAs are either passed or rejected, the on-chain NCL would quickly catch up to reality.

It might make sense to maybe rename the net change limit to net change threshold.

Regarding motivation:

> Memoization or tabulation algorithms

This is true for general programming but it's unclear whether any real validators, whose role is to validate transactions, require memoization or tabulation. Also, many such algorithms require a data structure that can store thunks and supports efficient indexing, which UPLC doesn't have (builtin Array doesn't fit because it cannot store thunks).

> Easier to write Haskell-like code

I like this motivation personally but it's quite specific to Plinth.

> Boehm-Berrarducci encodings and escape continuations

This is a useful example, but it's a bit too complex, with many details that may not be relevant. It would be better to extract a general argument, and use this example as concrete evidence.

With that said, I do think there's a decent motivation: I don't think laziness is strictly necessary to achieve low cost/size, but there's a good argument that it makes things more convenient. How about the following:

**1. Convenience**. To reuse the example I mentioned above: suppose there is a large and expensive expression that is used in two of the three branches, and in one of the branches it is used twice. In this case, you can indeed avoid duplicating code or work without laziness:

```
     let x = delay expensive in
     case scrut of
       A -> ... force x ...
       B -> let y = force x in ... y ... y ...
       C -> ...
```

but this is cumbersome and not ergonomic, not to mention that some surface languages may not even have delay/force constructs, making it impossible to write this code (I think this is the case with Aiken, but I'm not certain). Users would much rather write something like this (_not just in Plinth but in any surface language_):

```
     let x = lazy expensive in
     case scrut of
       A -> ... x ...
       B -> ... x ... x ...
       C -> ...
```

But if there's no laziness in UPLC, the burden would be on the compiler to optimize the latter into the former. I don't think any current compiler does this, and indeed, doing so is non-trivial (it would require a number of analyses, some of which may not be decidable) and may not preserve semantics. With lazy delay/force this becomes much easier.

I think the BB encoding example is a specific, concrete example of this argument.

**2. Code reuse**. Here's a [blog post by Augustsson](https://augustss.blogspot.com/2011/05/more-points-for-lazy-evaluation-in.html) that @effectfully pointed to me before, which argues that "Strict evaluation is fundamentally flawed for function reuse". Although validators are relatively small programs, code reuse is still very much relevant: the validation logic can frequently be expressed as a composition of list filtering, mapping, small predicates etc. Manually inlining or fusing things makes validators harder to audit and more prone to bugs.

A number of general-purpose strict languages also support limited form of laziness (e.g., Scala and OCaml), likely due to reasons similar to 1 and 2. In particular, here's an example used by "Functional Programming in Scala" to motivate lazy lists:

```scala
List(1, 2, 3, 4).map(_ + 10).filter(_ % 2 == 0).map(_ * 3)
```

**3. Some related discussions/comments in the Cardano community.**
- https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/issues/7018#issuecomment-2802923673

In order to ensure convergence I’d like to describe formally how I interpret pipelining. If this matches your understanding then I’ll add it to the CIP text.

---

Protocol pipelining with a factor N runs N instances of a mini-protocol on a single multiplexer subchannel for the given protocol ID. Each instance tracks its own state and agency as per the specification. One protocol state is marked as the switch state; the switch state must be one in which the initiator has agency. The subchannel is governed by a pair of multiplexers, one for sending and one for receiving, that behave in round-robin fashion across the N instances, starting at the first instance. Requests from the node are forwarded by the sending multiplexer to the currently selected instance and sending the resulting protocol message to the network; whenever having sent a message from the switch state, the send multiplexer selects the next instance. The receive multiplexer forwards received messages from the network to the currently selected protocol instance; whenever receiving a message that transitions that instance into the switch state, the receive multiplexer selects the next instance.

---

This implies that pipelining only works for miniprotocols which have a suitable switch state in which the initiator decides what to do next and the responder then can send one or more messages to get back to the switch state. A protocol in which the initiator would need to send again from a different intermediate state would not support pipelining (such protocols don’t yet exist in the Ouroboros family).

I don't have time to read the proposal right now, but happy to share some initial thoughts just based on your PR summary;

To me, this doesn't materially alleviate the "bad" parts of contention; indeed, I believe your proposal makes both worse. Whether it's not this is actually true, or whether it is worth it on other grounds, I will reserve judgement until I get time to read your proposal.

To me, there are two closely intertwined "bad" properties of contention:

- As a UX consideration, it forces a user to re-sign their transaction; in particular, this is only made worse by your proposal. In the current model, at the very least if I get my transaction into the mempool early, I can be fairly confident it'll settle; and me and others can build transactions that chain off of it. In your proposal, any transaction spending a contentious UTxO can be pre-empted, making it more common that I have to re-submit, and it breaks entire chains of transactions.
- Second, contention creates fairness problems; in classical finance terms, it ensures the market provides different spreads to different classes of users. Users with access to more sophisticated technology (automated bots, hot-keys for resigning, better mempool monitoring, better connection within the network, get better access to those UTxOs, and thus get an economic advantage. Automated trading bots get dibs on the best opportunities, while average users are pushed towards worse prices. In an orderbook, for example, the UX burden pushes users towards placing limit orders, rather than matching against the best bid/ask, and they get traded against by those sophisticated bots. Your proposal doesn't ameliorate this. On the one hand, it does make this advantage more expensive to exploit, but that benefit shifts to the network, not the "average" user.

Thus, if protocols (like Sundae) want to maintain a structural fairness and nice UX for all users, they're pushed towards protocols that avoid contention (perhaps even more strongly!)

Now, maybe that's fine; those protocols continue to remain unchanged, and other protocols accept this structural imbalance, and at least the network benefits from it, but it doesn't materially lesson the "problems" of contention.

And, at the very least (and maybe you mention this in your writeup), it should be sophisticated enough for the mempool to consider the *chain* of transactions it's replacing, not just an individual transaction, so that earning 0.1 extra ADA on a transaction doesn't cause the network to lose 20 ada worth of fees from the whole chain :sweat_smile:

@Quantumplation Both of your concerns are directly addressed by the mechanics of a localized fee market, and I think the fear of endless bidding wars might be a bit overstated. Consider the following:

1. The retail user is in full control of how much they overpay upfront.
2. Outside of high-value arbitrage/liquidations, bots tend to "penny-pinch" to preserve their margins. Because they can easily retry transactions, they are mathematically better off keeping their bids small.

A retail user can take advantage of this characteristic for scenarios where they desperately need a contentious UTxO. If the user overpays by 5x-10x (so a standard 0.5 ADA fee becomes 2.5-5.0 ADA), they are very likely to win the "auction." It is like a real-world auction where everyone is incrementing by $1, and suddenly someone increments by $100. At that point, the room usually folds. 

The eUTxO situation actually makes this even better because many of these contested resources are "continuing UTxOs" where the resource is immediately made available again after the current tx. When a bot sees a 5x retail bid, the rational, margin-optimizing choice isn't to start a bidding war—it's to let that UTxO go and just grab the next one in the subsequent block for a fraction of the cost. 

A retail user choosing to pay 2.5-5.0 ADA for guaranteed priority does not mean "only the rich can play." A huge reason bidding wars get so toxic on other chains is collateral damage: normal transactions get caught in the crossfire and have to bid for global block space. This CIP's targeted fee market confines the bidding *only* to the specific resource in question, meaning there is no extraneous bidding pushing up the price for the rest of the network. Instead of one giant auction, you have many small auctions:  one UTxO can have a 15 ADA bid while another one could have a 1.5 ADA bid.

Also, this may be a controversial take, but IMHO tx chain fees **should not** be considered when deciding the auction winner. Auction theory seems pretty clear about this.

**Bundling auctions reduces revenue.** The whole point of this CIP is that each contested UTxO gets its own independent auction. Counting descendant fees undermines that by merging separate auctions into one.

Consider a continuing UTxO that cycles four times. Without chaining in the fee comparison, each cycle gets its own auction. If each attracts a 15 ADA bid, the network earns 60 ADA. With chaining, all four cycles are bundled under a single replacement threshold. A chain paying 20 ADA total across all four beats out individual 15 ADA bids on each — the network earns 20 ADA instead of 60. Separate auctions over independent resources yield at least as much total revenue as bundled ones. This is a standard result in auction theory, and continuing UTxOs are the dominant case for DeFi contention.

**It also misprices demand.** This fee market prices UTxO contention *right now*. A transaction chain spreads its fees across future blocks. Requiring a challenger to outbid the next few hours of activity is not pricing current demand, it is creating a market inefficiency by ignoring the time-value of money.

If we don't consider tx chain fees, then we need a way to protect against ddos since these txs are fully validated but dropped before their fees are collected. Bitcoin caps the max chain depth but it doesn't have plutus script validation. So my current thought is a compromise: If Tx B conflicts directly with Tx A and Tx A has descendants, use the absolute fee for Tx A but only the required minimum fees for each descendant.

```
Replacement Rule:
fee(B) > fee(A) + minFee(B) + totalMinFee(descendants(A))
```

The fee of Tx B only needs to cover the lost validation work of the descendants, not outbid them. This separates the auctions as much as possible while still protecting against ddos.

Thanks for merging Thomas! Since it doesn’t make sense to continue the conversation in the other PR, I’ll write a summary here. Compact integer encoding, tagged sum types for questions (including a new ranking type), `(TxId, index)` survey references for batching, simplified identity via `required_signers`, and a cancellation mechanism. You will find a very minimal proof of concept on Preview with the updated CDDL spec here: https://cip-179-poc.pages.dev/ The source code there: https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cardano-governance-voting-tool/tree/minimal/minimal/src I have two main questions left: 1. Should we support decimal numbers instead of only integers for the numeric poll? 2. The survey has currently only a "maxRanked" parameter, to limit the max number of item ranked in a full list. I think a "minRanked" parameter would also make sense, as a limit of the minimum count of ranked choices. Think "rank at least 3 of these options from best to worst". I’d especially welcome @thenic95 @ptrdsh feedback on that point, since as I understand, Orion/CF could be the first creator of such a poll with ranking?

Both are worth adding.

For numeric polls, support decimals. Integer-only is too restrictive for real governance use cases like percentages, rates, or parameter tuning. Use a step field to control precision instead of a boolean flag, so integer-only is just step: 1, while decimals can be step: 0.1, 0.01, etc.

For ranked polls, add minRanked. maxRanked alone only limits over-ranking, but without minRanked you can’t require meaningful participation like “rank at least 3 options.” Together they form a complete constraint model, with minRanked ≤ maxRanked.

Recommendation: let's also bump the version number, since a poll has already been submitted on mainnet and this introduces a schema change that should be versioned explicitly.

Thank you for starting this CPS! 
Its obviously relevant... but also highly timely - perhaps more so than we think. 

I strongly believe we would benefit greatly as ecosystem from adding PQ _mitigation_ (not final solutions) already in Dijkstra, or at least into Euler (afaik thats the name for the next-next HF). Those mitigations could be kill switches, or expensive PQ solutions (which we I THINK already have in a way through Plutus scripts with hash-based spending rules, right?), but sending the signal of partial or optional readiness over just a roadmap is extremely valuable. 

___
Regardless of perception, I would like to share an approach for (partial) mitigation by the Bitcoin community, which I found insightful, and might be interesting for Cardano, as it addresses all three key types: 

Their work includes a kill switch (basically BIP 361) for user funds to block spending outputs that are based on simple signatures... 
... but then also to unlock those funds by proving ownership through ZK : 
1. utxos effectively get censored by SPOs if they rely on just an ECDSA sig to spend them. (or spending gets disallowed after epoch x on protocol level) 
2. Now fortunately, the majority of funds are sitting on addresses that are derived from a seed using BIP32/CIP-1852/ 1853 and 1854. Also fortunately, BIP32 derivation includes running the seed through a hash function before deriving child keys for usage in addresses. As @perturbing wrote in the CPS, current Quantum Computing (predominantly relying on Shor's algorithm) does not crack common hashing functions (there is Grover's algorithm, but it reduces the hash bits from 256 to 128, but that is high enough still). Since QC only cracks elliptic curve cryptography, not hashes, it is impossible to derive the seed from an exposed pubkey.
3. With that "lucky circumstance", there now exists a neat way to unlock those censored ECDSA utxos after a kill switch is activated: The owner of that utxo can create a ZK proof that they derived the exposed public key from their seed using BIP32 and can thus prove they are the rightful owner and spend that utxo. 
4. Problem is only: where should they spend it to? Once it is spent, the utxo would be exposed to the same situation as before.2 solutions:
- the pubkey is exposed only with the spending signature, and an address is the result of a hash, which is not vulnerable, so always using an address exactly once would already work as mitigation. 
- Or: make use of Plutus and spend "ECDSA utxos" that got unlocked with ZK-HD-proofs into script-addresses that require some hash to spend.

The bitcoin approach is indeed a known way to "upgrade", but sadly it only works/is secure for BIP32 (hash-based) derived keys. The keys that are generated via the CLI (or do not follow BIP32) cannot produce a seed phrase (this is really impossible). A few other hurdles with this approach, though a quantum-secure proof system exists, are that these are also not battle-tested. Here the risk is that a ZKP is underconstrained or even the soundness of the proving method is broken (so agility is here also a must). Then there is also the problem that different hardware wallets derive keys differently (ever tried to load a key from a Trezor to a Ledger? :smirk: ). There is no one-size-fits-all.

> In my mind, next steps should be defining or agreeing on what the goals and non-goals are,

I think this is why we have written this CPS, and just to reiterate our position. The weakest link is consensus; if that breaks, all bets are off. 

That is why plutus is out of scope (it has entirely different design principles and security models). Also, the first thing at risk is the consensus model. For plutus, I do have an idea for a quick fix, which is adding a SHA512 primitive. This way one can encode the public key hash via that and rotate it for every witness in the plutus script.  This would work for all signature schemes Plutus currently supports but does mean a more impactful rewrite of scripts.

As to the goals on consensus, I think the problem is threefold: the signatures for spending/governance/spo operation, etc. (all ed25519 based), the VRF leader schedule primitive (breaks adaptive security if QC attacks it); and lastly, the KES key, which ensures forward security to the chain. Note that the latter is also impactful, as we cannot retrospectively use different keys from past forged blocks; that is, we have to accept that a QC adversary can break this forward security, meaning another approach for safe bootstrapping a new node has to be found.

Also note, a CPS is not there to give a solution but to describe the problem :+1:  

So as an overview

>Are we trying to find a solution for coins that are sitting on vulnerable addresses?

Yes, that is in scope in this problem statement (this CPS does not describe how to solve it).

> for those that re-use addresses deliberately?

Yes

>for those that inadvertadly ignore every and all migration advice (or simply those coins that are lost)?

Good question; currently the CPS does not describe the details of a transition. I'll extend the CPS to scope out more about the details of a transition (and what questions will pop up like yours).

> the aspect about VRF and KES being vulnerable prob separates that question about catering to vulnerability further than just end-user issues, as those two are systemic risks and not just a matter of personal security.
>
>Or are we just trying to find [signatures, address-formats, logic, solutions] that are PQ resistant?

Note that the problem is equal in parts; both the spending issue and consensus break major protocol guarantees. A user is not secure if only one is solved. Thus, this CPS addresses both! Note that 3 CIPs that address each of the 3 parts (Ed25519 / VRF / KES) individually can happen.

Agreed on the unpredictability of ZK ownership proofs with the BTC method (albeit we can heavily rely on research done there to mitigate some of the unconstrained risks, etc.), but indeed, the method has its flaws, which includes complicated derivation differences, as well as "raw" HD-less keys and other subsets of all assets that are not included.

The reason I brought it up in a CPS and in connection with the goal- and non-goals question is that I believe specifically the transitioning part from ed25519-sig protected addresses to hash- or lattice-based-sig protected keys/addresses is a non-trivial, if perhaps not impossible task, because we simply cant force the transition for users. (this is why i asked Are we trying to find a solution for coins that are sitting on vulnerable addresses?).
Note that I do not mean the providing of a transition recommendation, or the providing of transition targets (such as addresses on a new address/key-format), which are obviously part of the goals, but specifically whether it is our (us being "people working towards Cardano PQ") task to protect vulnerable assets at rest, or those that are lost/eternally abandoned, as this type of problem is in a different category to upgrading to PQ, and should perhaps even get a different CPS.

If we, as a result of a potential impossibility are forced to exclude the transition for end-users from the goals of the making Cardano quantum-secure (not unreasonable in my mind), then especially it should go into a different CPS, as the metric for solutions/CIPs built out of such a problem statement would be % of unprotected assets protected, and include different discussions and considerations - especially also on social consensus levels.

I think differentiating this frees us from looking forward unconstrained.

Thank you for the detailed review. After thinking carefully about all the 
feedback, we decided to make some significant changes and resubmit.

Changing suffix from .id to .did (Decentralized Identifier)

This eliminates all conflicts with existing ADA Handle .id handles. The 
.did suffix aligns with the W3C DID specification 
(https://www.w3.org/TR/did-core/) -the globally recognized standard for 
decentralized identity. We feel this actually makes our proposal stronger 
and positions GetMyID as Cardano's native implementation of that standard 
rather than just another naming service.

2. Open participation framework

Fair point - we agree a single entity should not exclusively control a 
namespace. The revised CIP will define an open protocol where any 
qualified entity can issue .did handles, with Policy ID registration as 
the disambiguation mechanism. GetMyID would submit the first Policy ID 
as the reference implementation.

Individual author credits

Will be updated as requested - our mistake.

 Reprogramming our platform

We are also committed to updating our live platform at getmyid.today to 
use the .did suffix across the entire application before resubmitting.

Before we close this PR and start working on the revision - has anyone 
already claimed or proposed the .did suffix on Cardano? We want to make 
sure the namespace is clear before investing the work into the revised 
specification.

Thanks again for the time and patience, this feedback has been really 
valuable.

However, I want to raise a concern that I think is fundamental to this 
entire discussion — and not just for my proposal, but for any future 
naming standard on Cardano.

Even if ADA Handle confirms today that they have no .did handles and 
agree not to mint them — there is nothing technically stopping them from 
changing that decision tomorrow. If they later mint .did handles under 
their Policy ID and wallet teams integrate their Policy ID first due to 
their existing relationships and community presence, all users who already 
purchased .did handles from GetMyID would effectively have broken handles. 
Their handles would resolve to the wrong address or not resolve at all in 
wallets that prioritize ADA Handle's Policy ID.

This is not a hypothetical — it is exactly what would happen. And it 
would be the legitimate GetMyID users who suffer the consequences, not us.

This is precisely why I believe this CIP — or a CPS as you suggest — 
needs to define a proper hierarchy and governance framework for namespace 
ownership on Cardano BEFORE any more naming platforms are built. Without 
it, every new naming project is building on sand.

I am fully committed to contributing to that framework. But I also want 
the community to acknowledge that the current situation — where a well-funded 
incumbent can simply claim any suffix at any time with no governance 
mechanism to prevent it — is fundamentally unfair to new entrants who go 
through the proper CIP process in good faith.

What protections can the CIP process actually offer to prevent this scenario?

Thank you for this incredibly thoughtful and detailed response and for tagging the relevant stakeholders. This is exactly the kind of conversation Cardano needs to have.

I want to be transparent about my position: I came here to propose a simple naming standard, but this discussion has shown me that the real problem is much bigger - Cardano has no open governance framework for handle namespaces at all. ADA Handle built a monopoly with Catalyst funding and no open standard, no CIP, no community input. That is the root problem.

So here is what I am proposing to do:

1. Contribute the technical framework

I am willing to put in the work to draft a proper technical governance framework for handle namespace management on Cardano not just for GetMyID, but as a true open standard that any entity can participate in. This is clearly something the ecosystem needs and has never had. I will draft this as a CPS first as suggested.

2. Claim .did as the reference implementation

As the entity proposing and building this open framework, I believe it is fair and logical that GetMyID's Policy ID is registered as the primary reference implementation for the .did namespace - the first entry in the registry we are about to define together. Not because we own it exclusively, but because we are the ones doing the work to establish the standard.

This is how open source works in every other ecosystem, the entity that does the work of defining and implementing the standard earns the right to be the reference implementation. Apache, Linux, Ethereum -- all started this way.

3. On-chain registry as the solution

The protection I was asking about earlier does not need to come from the CIP process, it can come from an on-chain registry of approved namespace providers, governed by the framework we define in this CPS/CIP. Any wallet resolving .did handles would consult this registry. ADA Handle or any other entity that wants to participate would need to register and follow the governance rules, they cannot simply claim the namespace outside the framework.

This makes the system both open AND protected. No monopolies, no surprises for users, and clear rules for everyone.

4. Regarding the Cardano Foundation

I strongly welcome CF involvement here. Given that "Cardano" and "Ada" are CF trademarks, they have both the interest and the authority to ensure that identity infrastructure on Cardano is governed fairly and openly. I hope the CF representatives tagged here will engage with this discussion.

I want to be honest with the community about something: I am an independent developer financing this entire project out of my own pocket with no external funding, no Catalyst grants, no investors. I built GetMyID alone because I believed Cardano needed a fair, open identity solution. I am not a well-funded corporation - I am a single person who cares about this ecosystem enough to do the work and go through the proper process. That is exactly why fair governance matters so much to me. The current situation where a well-funded incumbent can claim any namespace at any time without governance is not just unfair to me, it is unfair to every future independent developer who tries to build on Cardano.

I am ready to do the work. The question is whether the community and the CF are ready to support a truly open identity framework for Cardano, one that finally gives this ecosystem what ADA Handle never provided.

After considering this proposal further, supporting parameter validation with _arbitrary shape_ does not seem to be of great benefit (which is where [the current solution](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/aiken-design-patterns/blob/82bdbdfc727388d048f12c0a069d197bf9ffb477/lib/aiken-design-patterns/parameter-validation.ak#L170-L188) proves too clunky).

As a short re-iteration, said solution requires scripts to be applied with a hashed parameter, and have the pre-image provided via the redeemer in any endpoint that needs access to it.

However, I'm now thinking scripts that need to validate instantiations of other parameterized scripts will most likely be able to be smart about it, and just use a hash without ever requiring its pre-image.

Meaning, by [simple bytestring manipulations](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/aiken-design-patterns/blob/82bdbdfc727388d048f12c0a069d197bf9ffb477/lib/aiken-design-patterns/parameter-validation.ak#L83-L97) (detailed [here](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/design-patterns/blob/62d97c1a32a040b877f7d78cc915d9c788bc9a89/parameter-validation/PARAMETER-VALIDATION.md)) we have a cheap solution, which its only downside could be developer-unfriendliness.

To demonstrate "developer-unfriendliness," I can point to how we've used it in Midgard:
- [The parameterized script itself](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/midgard/blob/15361d94a1180c51d957cc8e4bc53a5231568b71/onchain/aiken/validators/user-events/witness.ak)
- [Its generated CBOR bytes prefix](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/midgard/blob/15361d94a1180c51d957cc8e4bc53a5231568b71/onchain/aiken/env/default.ak#L63-L64) and [a temporary AI script](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/midgard/blob/staging/scripts/generate-user-events-witness-script-prefix.sh) that generates it
- [Validation of a resulting script hash](https://github.com/Anastasia-Labs/midgard/blob/15361d94a1180c51d957cc8e4bc53a5231568b71/onchain/aiken/lib/midgard/user-events.ak#L136-L143)

All in all, it seems we can either close this CIP, or keep it open in the hopes that at some point implementing this would be easy enough that its benefits would out-weigh its effort.

Thank you for opening this discussion. I agree that human-readable address resolution is important for Cardano, and I agree that wallets should have deterministic, safe, and user-friendly behavior when multiple naming systems exist.

Where I disagree is with the framing that the absence of a namespace-governance framework is itself the core problem, or that a CPS/CIP should become the mechanism by which namespace authority, suffix priority, or commercial legitimacy is assigned.

I think it is important to separate two very different goals:

1. **Resolver interoperability** — common metadata, provider identification, policy ID verification, collision warnings, wallet display guidance, security expectations, and user-choice mechanisms.
2. **Namespace allocation/governance** — deciding who has authority over `.id`, `.did`, or any other suffix, and determining which provider receives resolution priority.

I strongly support the first. I do not believe the second belongs in the CIP process.

## The market has already been the governance mechanism

ADA Handle did not receive its position through a CIP, committee, license, or official namespace grant. It competed in an open market.

Before ADA Handle reached broad adoption, Cardano already had competing naming approaches. AdaDomains pursued an earlier, more domain-like architecture using Cardano native assets and smart-contract functionality. ADA Handle took a different approach: make ownership and resolution much simpler.

In ADA Handle’s model, the handle is an NFT. Ownership is proven by possession of that NFT, and resolution is based on where that NFT currently resides. That simplicity made integration easier for wallets, dApps, explorers, marketplaces, and users.

The result was not imposed by governance. It was selected by the market.

ADA Handle’s adoption came from product-market fit, simple implementation, and extensive integration work with wallets and dApps. That is how permissionless ecosystems are supposed to work.

This does not mean ADA Handle should be protected from competition. The opposite is true. If GetMyID, CNS, Unstoppable Domains, or any other provider builds a better product and earns user and wallet adoption, Cardano benefits. Competition forces everyone to improve.

But competition should happen through better products, better integrations, better security, and better user experience — not through a retroactive standards process that reassigns namespace legitimacy.

## A CIP should not retroactively import DNS-style hierarchy into a flat NFT naming system

A major conceptual issue here is that suffixes such as `.id` or `.did` are being treated as if they are inherently hierarchical namespaces.

That is not how ADA Handle was designed.

ADA Handle asset names can contain characters such as periods. In that model, a dot is not automatically a delegated namespace boundary. A handle ending in `.did` is not necessarily a claim to operate a DNS-style `.did` namespace. It is a handle minted under a specific policy ID according to that provider’s rules.

Under a different naming architecture, suffixes may be meaningful namespaces. That is fine. But it is not appropriate to retroactively apply that architecture to existing minted assets and then classify earlier mints as namespace claims or squatting under rules that did not exist at the time.

On the specific `$did` issue: `$did` was minted under ADA Handle in March 2022 during ADA Handle’s mainnet launch period, not in response to this 2026 CPS discussion. To my knowledge, it has not been listed for sale. Treating that mint as evidence of reactive namespace squatting is factually incorrect and should be corrected or removed from the CPS.

## The CIP process cannot solve this by assigning authority

The CPS itself acknowledges that participation in the CIP process is voluntary and that a CIP/CPS cannot prevent anyone from minting handles in any format.

That limitation is not incidental. It is the core issue.

If this CPS leads to a registry that existing providers are expected to obey voluntarily, then it cannot actually prevent parallel systems from existing. If wallets enforce that registry anyway, then wallets may break or deprioritize existing user expectations. If some wallets enforce the registry and others do not, Cardano ends up with more fragmentation, not less.

The likely result would be:

- ADA Handle resolution
- CNS resolution
- Unstoppable Domains resolution
- GetMyID or registry-based resolution
- Future provider-specific resolution systems

That is not unification. It is another resolution regime layered on top of the ones that already exist.

Yoroi’s public support for ADA Handle, CNS, and Unstoppable Domains already demonstrates the practical reality: wallets can and do support multiple naming providers. The right standard should help wallets do that safely and transparently, not try to decide which provider deserves namespace authority.

## User protection requires backward compatibility

Any standard in this area must put existing users first.

Users purchased or minted handles under the rules of the provider they used. Wallets and dApps integrated those providers according to their known policy IDs and resolution behavior. A later governance framework should not change those expectations retroactively.

A safe standard should include explicit non-goals:

- It should not retroactively reassign suffix authority.
- It should not make existing handles unresolvable.
- It should not require existing providers to give up already-minted names.
- It should not define “reference implementation” status in a way that grants commercial or resolution priority to the author of the CPS/CIP.
- It should not make a centralized or committee-based process the arbiter of namespace legitimacy.

## A better path: resolver interoperability, not namespace allocation

I would support reframing this CPS toward resolver interoperability.

A useful standard could define:

- provider identity metadata;
- policy ID verification;
- resolver metadata format;
- wallet display rules, including “resolved via ADA Handle,” “resolved via CNS,” etc.;
- collision detection;
- user warnings when the same visible name exists under multiple providers;
- user-configurable resolver preferences;
- homograph and phishing protections;
- provider deprecation metadata;
- voluntary migration mechanisms;
- backwards compatibility expectations.

That would address the real wallet UX problem without creating a new namespace authority.

The goal should be that wallets can safely resolve names from multiple providers while making the provider and policy ID clear to the user. If there is ambiguity, wallets should warn rather than silently choosing a winner.

## Suggested change to the CPS framing

I would suggest changing the problem statement from:

> Cardano lacks a governance framework for handle namespaces.

to something closer to:

> Cardano lacks a common resolver-interoperability framework for wallets and dApps that need to support multiple naming providers safely, transparently, and without breaking existing users.

That is a technical problem. It belongs in the CIP process.

By contrast, deciding who controls `.id`, `.did`, or any other suffix is not merely a technical problem. It is a governance and market-allocation question. CIP-1 is clear that the CIP process does not itself provide governance.

## Closing position

ADA Handle is not asking the CIP process to protect it from competition. New providers should be free to build, mint, integrate, and persuade users.

But permissionless competition does not guarantee every entrant the namespace they prefer. It guarantees every entrant the right to build, compete, integrate, and earn adoption.

A naming system should earn resolution priority through user adoption, wallet implementation, technical quality, and trust — not through a retroactive standards process.

I would be much more comfortable with this CPS if it were narrowed to resolver interoperability, collision handling, user protection, and backward compatibility, while explicitly excluding retroactive namespace allocation or provider-priority assignment.

I want to clarify what I believe this CPS should produce, because I think it will help focus the discussion.

I am not asking for GetMyID to be given special treatment. I am proposing a two-layer standard:

Layer 1 - A Framework CIP that defines:
- The process any naming provider must follow to register a namespace
- The technical criteria they must meet
- The resolver specification format wallets must implement
- How resolution priority is determined when conflicts exist
- How registered namespaces are protected from being claimed by others

Layer 2 — Individual Provider CIPs where each naming platform 
submits their own CIP declaring:
- Their namespace format
- Their Policy ID
- Their resolver endpoint
- Their compliance with the Framework CIP

Once a provider's individual CIP is accepted, their namespace is formally recognized and wallets that want to be considered 
Cardano-compatible are expected to implement their resolver.

The critical rule that makes this work:

The FIRST provider to have their individual CIP accepted by the community for a specific namespace format gets PRIMARY resolution for that namespace. This means:

- If GetMyID submits a CIP for .did and it is accepted, GetMyID's Policy ID becomes the primary resolver for .did handles
- If ADA Handle or any other entity later wants to mint handles ending in .did, wallets will by default resolve .did to GetMyID's Policy ID — because GetMyID went through the formal process first
- ADA Handle is free to mint .did handles under their Policy ID - but those handles will not receive primary wallet resolution 
  because they did not go through the governance process for that namespace

This is exactly how ENS works on Ethereum. The ENS contract is the primary resolver for .eth names. Anyone can build a competing system but wallets resolve .eth through ENS by default because ENS defined the standard.

This means:
- ADA Handle submits an individual CIP for their $name namespace - their Policy ID gets primary resolution for that format
- GetMyID submits an individual CIP for .did — our Policy ID gets primary resolution for .did
- Any future developer submits an individual CIP for their chosen namespace — they get primary resolution for that namespace
- No entity can claim primary resolution for a namespace they did not register through the formal process — regardless of how many handles they minted under that format

Regarding the suggestion that Kora should hand the ADA Handle standard to Cardano governance — I fully support that idea and it is completely compatible with this proposal. Under the two-layer framework, ADA Handle submitting their standard to Cardano governance IS their Layer 2 CIP submission. The governance framework this CPS 
proposes is the mechanism through which that handover would happen in a structured and protected way.

No private relationships required. No incumbent advantage. Just a transparent technical process that any qualified developer can follow.

This is how every mature blockchain ecosystem handles naming standards. ENS on Ethereum has a defined standard. Unstoppable Domains has a defined standard. Cardano should too.

Right now neither layer exists. My CPS is asking the community to build Layer 1. Once that exists, I will immediately submit Layer 2 for GetMyID — and I would strongly encourage ADA Handle and CNS to do the same.

I want to be clear about one final point: this process is not retroactive and does not break anything for existing users. ADA 
Handle users keep their handles. CNS users keep their handles. GetMyID users keep their handles. The Framework CIP applies going forward — it defines the rules for new namespace registrations and gives wallets a standard to implement. Nothing breaks. Nobody loses anything. Everyone gains clarity.

The address-derivation procedure has been restructured into a byte-level function **R** (4 new commits).

**Core benefit: TOA addresses are now derivable on-chain by other validators.** Plutus V3 exposes no primitive that applies parameters to an unapplied script and serialises the result, so under `apply_params + ledger_serialise` no on-chain code could derive a TOA address. R closes that gap using only `appendByteString`, `consByteString`, `lengthOfByteString`, `serialiseData`, `blake2b_224`. A generic validator can now check *"is this output at the TOA for the NFT in this transaction?"* without being pre-parameterised per controlling NFT — one deployed validator serves every TOA. (R is also implementable in any off-chain language with bytestring concatenation and blake2b-224, ~50 lines, no Plutus tooling.)

**Technical cost.** TOA v1's validator was recompiled to accept `BuiltinData` so parameters delivered as a `Constant Data` UPLC term (`cardano-api`'s `applyArguments` semantics) execute correctly. Predicate logic and trace codes unchanged — all 38 CLB validator scenarios still pass — but every `expected_script_hash` and `expected_address_*` differs from 0.1.1. TOA v1 is `Proposed` with no mainnet deployments; the address change is in-scope.

R is content-hashed at [en7angled/toa@0.2.0](https://github.com/en7angled/toa/releases/tag/0.2.0); [`toa-verify-reconstruction`](https://github.com/en7angled/toa/blob/0.2.0/src/exe/toa-verify-reconstruction/Main.hs) empirically proves R reproduces `apply_params + ledger_serialise` byte-for-byte. The conformance-vs-documentation split from discussion_r3293465306 is preserved.

I want to add another framing that may help separate two different problems:

1. whether multiple naming / identity providers can coexist; and
2. whether Cardano needs a governance process to assign default namespace priority.

In the Web2 identity world, multiple handle and account systems coexist constantly.

People have identities on GitHub, Google, Discord, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, and many other platforms. Those platforms are not interchangeable, and nobody expects a global governance process to decide which provider owns a username across the entire internet.

The same visible username can exist on many services at the same time. `alice` on GitHub is not automatically the same person as `alice` on Discord, Instagram, X, or Google. That is not usually treated as a system failure. It is treated as provider context.

When a website supports external login, it does not ask a governance body to decide which provider is globally authoritative for the user. It presents the user with options:

- continue with Google;
- continue with GitHub;
- continue with Discord;
- continue with X;
- continue with some other provider;
- or use a local account.

That is a user-choice model.

OAuth and OpenID Connect work in this general shape. OAuth lets a third-party application obtain limited access after an approval interaction with the resource owner and authorization server. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 so a client can verify an end user’s identity based on authentication performed by an authorization server.

The important point is not that Cardano handles should literally copy OAuth or OIDC. The important point is architectural: mature identity ecosystems already tolerate multiple providers by making provider context explicit.

They do not require one global registry to decide that `alice` belongs to GitHub, Google, Discord, or LinkedIn everywhere.

## Provider context is not a flaw

A handle is not meaningful in isolation. It is meaningful inside a provider context.

For example:

- GitHub identity: `github.com/alice`
- Discord identity: `alice` on Discord
- X identity: `@alice`
- Instagram identity: `@alice`
- Google identity: a Google account
- ADA Handle identity: `$alice`
- CNS identity: a CNS name
- Unstoppable identity: an Unstoppable domain
- GetMyID identity: a GetMyID-issued identifier

These can coexist because the provider is part of the resolution context.

The Web2 solution to this is not universal username governance. It is provider-aware UX.

The same idea can apply here.

Wallets and dApps can support multiple Cardano naming providers without needing the CIP process to assign global priority over suffixes. They can expose provider context clearly and let users select the identity provider they intend to use.

## Default priority is not neutral

The argument has been made that “interoperability without resolution priority rules is incomplete.”

I disagree with that framing.

A default priority rule is not a purely technical detail. It is a market allocation decision. It decides which provider receives privileged wallet behavior when ambiguity exists.

That means the standard would not merely describe how providers interoperate. It would decide which provider wins when two providers can resolve the same visible string.

That is a much stronger claim than interoperability.

In the Web2 login model, a website does not need to decide that Google is the global default identity provider for all usernames. It can offer “Sign in with Google” next to “Sign in with GitHub” and let the user choose. GitHub’s own OAuth documentation says users can connect their GitHub identity to third-party applications using OAuth, and should review the application and requested access before authorizing. That is user consent and provider choice, not global provider priority.

## Human-readable does not have to mean providerless

A concern was raised that users should not need to know which provider issued a handle. I agree that UX should reduce burden on the user. But hiding provider context entirely can create a worse failure mode.

If multiple systems exist, pretending the provider does not matter is dangerous.

The provider determines:

- which policy ID is authoritative;
- which resolver rules apply;
- which ownership model applies;
- whether the name is an NFT, a contract entry, a domain-style record, or something else;
- what recovery, expiry, metadata, and transfer behavior exist;
- what trust assumptions the user is accepting.

That is material information.

Good UX should make this simple, not invisible.

For example, a wallet could show:

- `$alice` — ADA Handle
- `alice.did` — GetMyID
- `alice.blockchain` — Unstoppable Domains
- `alice` — CNS

Or, for ambiguous input, a wallet could show a provider picker:

> Multiple providers can resolve this name. Choose the provider you intend to use.

That is not a burden. That is informed consent.

## This is closer to identity-provider selection than DNS

The CPS discussion often compares the problem to DNS, ENS, and domain registries.

That analogy may be too narrow.

Cardano handle systems are not only domain systems. They are identity, payment, profile, and resolution systems. In that world, the better analogy may be external identity providers.

The web did not solve identity by creating one global username registry. It solved it by allowing many providers to coexist and by making provider selection explicit at the point of use.

That model has several advantages:

- no provider needs permission to exist;
- no governance process needs to allocate global username rights;
- users can maintain identities across many communities;
- applications choose which providers they support;
- providers compete on trust, usability, reach, security, and integrations;
- unpopular providers fade without requiring formal removal;
- successful providers gain adoption without needing official status.

That maps well to a public blockchain ecosystem.

## Application communities naturally form around providers

Users do not experience identity as one global namespace. They experience identity through communities.

A developer may be known by a GitHub handle.
A professional may be known by a LinkedIn profile.
A gamer may be known by a Discord identity.
A creator may be known by an Instagram or X handle.
A Cardano user may be known by an ADA Handle.
Another Cardano user may prefer CNS, Unstoppable, GetMyID, or some future naming system.

People move between communities. They keep multiple identities. Platforms rise and fall. Users choose where they want presence.

That is normal.

Trying to force all naming systems into one governed hierarchy risks imposing a DNS-style model onto a broader identity problem.

## What a CIP should standardize instead

A useful CIP could still exist here, but it should standardize provider-aware interoperability rather than namespace ownership.

For example:

- provider identifiers;
- policy ID verification;
- resolver metadata;
- wallet display format;
- collision warnings;
- user-selected default provider;
- payment URI parameters that specify provider context;
- safe fallback behavior;
- phishing / homograph warnings;
- how wallets should present ambiguous names;
- how dApps can request a specific provider;
- how providers publish resolver capabilities.

That would make the ecosystem safer without assigning namespace winners.

## Core point

Multiple providers are not the problem. Ambiguous, invisible provider context is the problem.

The solution should not be a governance process that assigns default namespace priority. The solution should be UX and resolver standards that make provider context explicit and user choice easy.

Cardano does not need to decide that one provider owns a suffix across the ecosystem. Wallets and dApps can support multiple providers the same way modern applications support multiple identity providers.

Let users choose. Let wallets disclose provider context. Let providers compete.
