1. I think you are misunderstanding how this CIP would work. It is just the normal fee mechanism which goes into the epoch's pot to be distributed with the next rewards. *It does not go directly to the producer who includes the tx.* This makes it agnostic to nested txs.
2. The mempool implementation is left out of the CIP, but the tx which pays more must cover all costs for all txs it replaces. So if a tx chain built up in the mempool on top of the dropped tx, the chain needs to be evicted too and the new tx needs to cover the total cost of the chain to prevent a DDoS scenario.
3. No, it is not automatically rejected. Are you sure you aren't over-complicating the "network of bids"? If tx A conflicts with *both* tx b and tx C, tx A must pay more than the sum of tx b and tx c. In practice, this means it will be hard to win auctions when you try taking multiple competitive UTxOs in one tx. If you challenge them one at a time, you might be fine with a small bid, but if they are all in the same mempool together, you will lose the auction. So you need to create a disproportionately large bid just in case. As a result, the revenue from this feature should more than compensate for the complexity of having to track evicting multiple tx chains at once.

This CPS is well-written and clearly identifies real tensions in the current design — but I believe it misdiagnoses them as problems to be solved, when they are actually features working as intended.

**Accountability is not a side effect of public voting. It is the entire point of DReps.**

DReps exist because not every ADA holder has the time or expertise to evaluate every governance action. Delegation is a trust relationship: delegators hand over their voting power in exchange for the expectation that the DRep will vote in a manner consistent with their stated values and commitments. The only mechanism that makes this trust relationship meaningful is verifiable accountability — delegators must be able to confirm how their DRep actually voted.

The CPS frames delegator pressure as "coercion." I would frame it differently: a large stakeholder threatening to redelegate if a DRep votes against their interests is the accountability mechanism functioning correctly. That is not a bug. That is a delegator exercising the one lever they have. Insulating DReps from that lever does not protect governance quality — it protects DReps from their own delegators.

## On the specific failure modes raised

**Vote-buying and coercion:** A DRep who can be bought is a problem regardless of whether their vote is visible. Vote privacy does not eliminate bribery; it makes it harder to verify that the bribe was honored, which may actually increase its prevalence.

**Herding and last-mover advantage:** This exists in every deliberative body, from legislatures to corporate boards. Observing how peers are leaning and adjusting one's position is called *deliberation*, not a failure mode. If a DRep changes their vote after seeing the trend, their delegators can observe that and draw their own conclusions.

**Cartel signaling:** Off-chain coordination is already possible and unstoppable. Private on-chain voting does not prevent cartels from forming; it just makes their coordination less legible to the outside.

**Chilling effect on minority positions:** This is a real concern, but the solution is better DRep culture and norms, not structural opacity. A DRep with a minority view should be able to articulate and defend it. If they cannot defend their vote publicly, that is relevant information for their delegators.

## The deeper problem with this proposal

Goal G2 — "preserve delegator accountability" — is listed as the second-highest priority, but every plausible solution to the stated problem directly undermines it. The open questions around selective disclosure, opt-in/opt-out mechanisms, and post-hoc reveals are attempts to square a circle. You cannot simultaneously hide a vote from "adversaries" and reliably surface it to delegators; the adversary and the delegator are often the same party.

If DRep votes are made private, delegators are left trusting that their DRep voted as promised, with no on-chain means of verification. At that point, the accountability relationship has been reduced to reputation and off-chain attestation. We could achieve that outcome far more simply by just not having DReps and running the governance system with direct weighted voting.

## Conclusion

The problems this CPS identifies — social pressure, strategic voting timing, coordination among large stakeholders — are real, but they are the natural dynamics of any representative system operating at scale. The correct response is to build norms, tooling, and community structures that help DReps navigate those dynamics with integrity, not to remove the transparency that makes accountability possible in the first place.

I do not believe a satisfactory solution to this problem statement exists that does not fatally compromise the DRep accountability model. I would recommend the CPS not progress in its current framing.

I want to clarify my position after the meeting because I think there is a middle ground between "governance hierarchy" and 
"pure user choice" that has not been fully explored.

I am not asking for mandatory governance. I am asking for a voluntary technical standard with a default resolution hint.

Here is the concrete proposal:

1. Any naming provider can register their namespace in a public on-chain registry by submitting a CIP defining:
   - Their namespace format (e.g. .did, .mmr, $name)
   - Their Policy ID
   - Their resolver endpoint

2. The registry records which provider registered a format first. That provider is flagged as the DEFAULT resolver for that format.

3. Wallets that implement this standard resolve to the default provider automatically — but ALWAYS show the user a provider    picker option so they can choose a different one if they want.

4. If a user types john.smith.did in a wallet:
   - Wallet checks the registry
   - Finds GetMyID registered .did first
   - Resolves to GetMyID by default
   - Shows user: "Resolved via GetMyID — tap to change provider"
   - User can switch to ADA Handle or any other provider if they want

This is identical to how browsers handle search engines -Chrome has a default search engine but users can change it 
at any time. Nobody calls that governance. It is just a sensible default with user override.

The registry itself requires no committee, no voting, no central authority. It is first-come-first-served based on CIP acceptance date. The CIP process already has a transparent, community-reviewed acceptance mechanism.

This satisfies both sides of the debate:

For @papag00se — user choice is always preserved

For me — a new provider who goes through the proper process gets a fair default resolution path without needing private 
wallet relationships

For wallets — a clear technical standard to implement

For users — simple default resolution with transparent provider context and easy override

I believe this is technically admissible as a CIP because it defines purely technical behavior - registry format, resolver API, wallet display rules, default selection logic - with no governance or authority assigned to any entity.

I am happy to draft this as a revised CPS focused purely on these technical elements if the editors agree this framing is acceptable.

@Cerkoryn — thank you for taking the time to read the CIP carefully and to lay out the comparison in chart form.  
The five-pool table is a good frame for the discussion and makes it easier to answer you precisely.  
Let me take your two questions in order.

## On your chart

Your math is correct. Under the proposal `A_new = A_current · u` with `u = S / S_sat`, so Pool 3 (`u = 0.5`) earns half of today's pledge bonus. Pool 3 is the right pool to focus on — same pledge as Pool 2, half the delegation, half the proposed bonus.

| Pool       | Scenario           | Current bonus | Proposed bonus            |
| ---------- | ------------------ | ------------: | ------------------------: |
| Pool 1     | P = 100%, S = 100% |          100% |                      100% |
| Pool 2     | P =  50%, S = 100% |           50% |                       50% |
| **Pool 3** | **P =  50%, S =  50%** |       **50%** | **25%**  ← *halved* |
| Pool 4     | P =   0%, S = 100% |            0% |                        0% |
| Pool 5     | P =   0%, S =  50% |            0% |                        0% |

## Your first question — *"it appears to make pledge less important and saturation the dominating factor. Or am I misunderstanding?"*

You understand correctly, and that effect is intentional. The CIP states it directly:

> Pledge becomes a partnership claim, redeemed by attracting delegation rather than declared in isolation.

An empty pledged pool earns nothing from pledge. A half-utilized one earns half. The whole point is to make pledge contingent on demonstrated demand. The saturation case is preserved exactly — a saturated pool earns today's bonus — so no SPO already running a popular pool loses anything.

## Your second question — about the operator

Your operator-side analysis lands. Per-ADA-pledge return is roughly preserved across pool sizes today, because pledge rewards flow back to the same operator (effectively fee-free), and margin plus fixed fee on additional delegators give the operator a slice of every new ADA arriving. I won't dispute that framing — it's a fair operator observation, and the CIP doesn't actually claim that operator dilution is the problem it solves.

But the dilution the CIP names lives on the *delegator* side, not the operator side. Appendix A.3's worked example uses a 50 M-pledge pool with `F = 340`, `r = 0.000400`:

- `S = 50 M` (pledge only): `(A − F)/S ≈ 8.55 × 10⁻⁵`
- `S = 75 M` (saturated): `(A − F)/S ≈ 5.70 × 10⁻⁵`

That's a **≈ 0.21% absolute ROA loss** absorbed by delegators for the act of arriving at the pool. Per-delegator ROA falls as delegation arrives at a high-pledge pool — the protocol's stated Nash equilibrium (CIP-0084) assumes delegators rotate toward high-pledge, well-operated pools, and today's formula penalizes them in exactly the regime they're supposed to prefer. Under the proposal `A/S` becomes independent of `S` and the slope flips positive everywhere.

To be fully candid: there are parameter regimes (low margin, low fee, high pledge) where the *operator's* income curve also dips when delegators arrive — the "red zone" in the simulator — but those aren't typical pool parameters, so the delegator dilution above is the load-bearing argument, not the operator one.

## Structural wins beyond dilution

Even granting your operator point in full, two structural wins remain that don't depend on operator dilution at all:

**1. Cooperative bargaining surface.** A coordinator (Pool Ranger, or any large delegator) lifts `A_new / S` for every existing delegator by arriving, and drops it visibly by leaving. The threat of withdrawal becomes a publicly computable mathematical event, giving SPOs a continuous incentive to *retain* large delegators, not just attract them.

**2. MPO deterrence at the formula level.** `a₀` is untouched, so Sybil resistance via delegator preference is preserved exactly as it stands. On top of that, the proposal adds a formula-level cost for splitting. For a 50 M ADA holder (`r = 0.000548`, `a₀ = 0.3`, `S_sat = 75 M`, self-funded splits):

```mermaid
xychart-beta
    title "Pledge bonus revenue — 50 M ADA holder, by strategy (K ADA/year)"
    x-axis "Strategy" ["Today (any N)", "Proposed N=1", "Proposed N=2", "Proposed N=10", "Proposed N=100"]
    y-axis "Annual pledge bonus (K ADA)" 0 --> 500
    bar [462, 308, 154, 31, 3]
```

A 10-way self-funded split costs roughly **277 K ADA/year** in forgone bonus versus staying in one pool; today it costs zero. The cost grows linearly with N, and the formula-level deterrent compounds with the existing delegator-preference channel.

These two wins hold whether or not operators are diluted today.

## A visual walkthrough, if you'd like to step through it

I've added a guided presentation to the interactive simulator that walks through your two questions card-by-card, loads Pool 3 into the chart so the halved bonus is visible on the metric cards, and steps through the responses above:

[https://johnshearing.github.io/pool_ranger/CIP_UTILIZATION_SCALED_PLEDGE_BONUS.html](https://johnshearing.github.io/pool_ranger/CIP_UTILIZATION_SCALED_PLEDGE_BONUS.html)

Click the button **"▶ A reviewer's questions about Pool 3 — answered card by card"** at the top, or press ▶ Play inside the card to let it run on its own. Eleven steps, ~2 minutes if autoplayed.

Thank you again for the careful read — your framing of Pool 3 sharpened the response, and I'd welcome any pushback on the delegator-side numbers or the MPO table, which are where the case actually lives.

Added `RegistrationMode { RegisterOnly | RegisterAndMint }` to `RegistryInsert`; cryptographic binding of `minting_logic_script` (replaces `hashed_param` in the redeemer); new `minting_logic_script` field on `RegistryNode`. Any objections about the approach taken? Does the shape look right to you?
- **F10 — Redundant single-mint check** ([#62](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/62), merged #68). **TL;DR:** `single_mint_with_credential` and the matching `minting_logic_cred` redeemer field added execution cost without security beyond what the policy-id derivation chain already enforces (so the field was redundant). Removed `minting_logic_cred` from the issuance redeemer; collapsed `SmartTokenMintingAction` wrapper to bare `MintingRegistryProof`. Any concerns about this becoming the spec-level wire format?

### 2. Open — feedback request

The following items are still in the pipeline and we could do with additional feedback from the working group on how to best move forward.

- **F11 — TransferAct composability** (Medium, [#63](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/63)). **TL;DR:** when a PLB UTxO holds multiple programmable tokens, every token's `transfer_logic_script` must be satisfied in the same transaction — conflicting rules can soft-lock the UTxO and can be weaponised by malicious tokens injected into a victim's wallet. Add a new PLGlobal redeemer variant for "pass-through" tokens (one programmable token transferred; others returned unchanged so their `transfer_logic_script` isn't invoked). Possible solution for busy utxos, but leaning towards `Unfracking`, see below.
- **F17 — Unconstrained asset addition / Unfracking** (Medium, [#72](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/72)). **TL;DR:** nothing bounds how many assets a smart-wallet UTxO can accumulate; bloated values inflate the execution cost of transfer and third-party paths and can effectively soft-lock the UTxO. Add an `Unfracking` PLGlobal redeemer variant so a holder can redistribute their own tokens across UTxOs without invoking transfer logic. Could be a good solution to break down large smart wallets utxos.
- **F18 — ThirdPartyAct admin scope is not clearly defined** (Informational, [#73](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/73)). **TL;DR:** `ThirdPartyAct` grants admin authority over any PLB UTxO that happens to hold the administered token — including DEX pools, lending collateral, and other DeFi-protocol UTxOs — which can deter DeFi integration: an admin could seize collateral, force liquidations, or block time-sensitive operations through the same path used for legitimate compliance. Should CIP-113 define and standardise an explicit (narrow) scope for admin authority, or leave the scope-bounding to each substandard? Either way, making the surface visible and bounded in the spec would help integrators reason about exposure.
- **F15 — Atomic multi-policy ThirdPartyAct** (Informational, [#67](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/67)). **TL;DR:** `ThirdPartyAct` resolves exactly one policy per invocation, so a compliance op that must atomically touch two policies at once (e.g. retire A+B, mint replacement C) cannot fit in a single tx. Reshape the `ThirdPartyAct` redeemer to `ThirdPartyAct { actions: List<(registry_node_idx, outputs_start_idx)> }` so one tx can act on multiple policies. Worth adopting, or out of scope?
- **F20 — Registry update / de-register lifecycle** (Informational, [#75](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues/75)). **TL;DR:** there is no way to update or de-register a registry node after the fact, so fixing a bug in a token's transfer/third-party logic — or exiting CIP-113 cleanly — is impossible without minting a new policy and migrating users. Introduce a `RegistryLifecycleAuthority` (the issuance-logic credential proves authority) and new redeemer variants for `Update` and `Deregister` (irreversible, flagged on the node rather than deleted). Introduces a certain level of upgradability, these findings could be adopted in part or as a whole.

### Closing note

This is only a subset of the audit findings — the items where a CIP-level call (or sanity check on an already-shipped one) would help most. The complete list, with severity, status, and links to the PRs that resolved them, lives on the [audit-finding issues page](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/cip113-programmable-tokens/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3Aaudit-finding). Anyone interested in the full picture is very welcome to browse there and follow the linked PRs for the resolutions.

Here are some lessons learned while integrating with wallets that we publish on our site https://handle.me/#verified_integration. This was curated after a few months of bad resolves (on the wallet side) and confused users. I will include the content here:

----
A "Verified Integration" must follow these best practices when a $handle is used to resolve an address:

- Do not rely solely on "debounce" techniques to resolve a $handle. This often resolves $handles incorrectly if the user continues typing after a debounce and the prior HTTP request is delayed. Instead, we’d prefer an explicit user action that indicates they are finished typing, like the "Enter" or "Tab" keys, clicking a button, or the input field "blur" event. If a "debounce" is used, then it should be double-checked after an explicit user action has taken place.
- Disable browser autofill on address input fields. Sometimes users inadvertently select autofill values from the browser if they are enabled. Please see [this post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64815751/disable-the-browser-autofill-on-input-fields-all-browsers) for more information.
- Have a visual display that the correct $handle was resolved. This can come in two forms (our favorite is both):
  - Repeat / Redisplay back to the user the $handle your code resolved. This acts as a confirmation that you resolved the $handle they expected you to.
OR
  - Display the $handle NFT image as another form of confirmation to the user that the correct $handle was resolved.
- Display a warning message if a $handle resolves to a script address. ESPECIALLY if there is no datum attached. Unless it is a multi-sig address, this is most certainly unwanted.
- On transaction review pages, reiterate the $handle name and/or NFT image, along with the address.
----

**On the "resolver endpoint"** - this should be reframed as **"resolution methods"** as on-chain resolution should be encouraged if not required, but "easier" API calls are also welcomed to facilitate ease-of-development. ADA Handles has both, including our own API. Maybe two (or more) fields for resolution method:
- "On-chain resolution"
- "API resolution"
- Other resolution methods (MCP, SDK, etc.)

**Concerning CPS-0008 and domain names** - Although there is a lot of overlap between domains and handles, and some products make them the same thing (like ENS), I think it is not beneficial to the community to treat them as the same thing. There are domain concerns, and there are handle concerns. Just as `x.com` (the domain) has millions of users - each with their own handles, so does, `facebook.com`, `github.com`, `instagram.com`, and many more. Handles identify a user within a community. A domain guides many users to, and defines a community.

This isn't to say that there can't be a CIP that attempts to address both, but they are different enough concerns that we may be trying to force a square peg into a round hole.

2. **`signature` / `walletKey` / `response` / `errorCode` / `errorMessage` not in ABNF `key` production** — §Response signing requires these on every response URL, but the URI-format ABNF rejects them as unknown keys under strict-decode. ABNF should be extended to enumerate response-only keys.

4. **§Callback host binding `-4` destination ambiguity** — spec doesn't say which host receives the rejection envelope when `redirect` host differs from `connect`-time binding.

6. **Witness-set merge for `partialSign=true`** — spec inherits CIP-30's flag verbatim but doesn't specify array-append semantics on map key 0 (vkey_witnesses). Suggest one paragraph.
7. **`extractTxBody` literal vs re-serialise** — spec mandates "canonical re-serialise" of element 0, but real Conway bodies must be the **literal** input bytes (BLAKE2b-256 over them == chain's `tx_id`). Suggest restating as "extract the literal tx_body bytes" with a note that the source CBOR is expected to already be canonical.
8. **§Response signing port inclusion** — spec doesn't say whether explicit port is part of canonical authority. Yuti includes it per RFC 3986 §3.2; suggest making this explicit.
9. **§Conway tx body extraction reference encoder** — spec says "canonical re-serialise" but doesn't pin a reference encoder; libraries vary on deterministic-only vs strictly-deterministic CBOR.

9-ambiguity bundle patch landed in commit [\`f76b5bf\`](https://github.com/Flux-Point-Studios/CIPs/commit/f76b5bf). 77 insertions / 25 deletions, all surgical, no semantic re-litigation outside the 9 listed items. Summary per ambiguity:

1. **Appendix C.1 nonce** — 36-char value → 32-char `AgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgIC` (24 bytes). Fixed in both the constant listing and the request-URL example.
2. **ABNF response-side keys** — split `key` into `request-key` and `response-key` productions. Adds `response`, `walletKey`, `nonce`, `payload`, `signature`, `errorCode`, `errorMessage` to the response side.
3. **ABNF `aead`** — added to `request-key` production (was missing despite being referenced in §Methods AEAD envelope).
4. **§Unknown-key policy** — now references both ABNF productions so the strict-reject rule applies symmetrically to wallets parsing requests and dApps parsing responses.
5. **§Callback host binding `-4` destination** — `errorCode=-4 RedirectHostMismatch` envelope MUST be delivered to the `connect`-time persisted `redirect`, NOT the offending request's `redirect`. Closes the cross-host phishing defeat where -4 would otherwise sink into the attacker's domain.
6. **§signTx `result-json.commit` echo** — promoted to MUST: dApp verifies echo equals request commit; mismatch is `errorCode=-2`. Defence-in-depth complement to the wallet's pre-render commit check.

8. **§Conway tx body extraction** — literal-bytes rule. Wallet MUST slice the source CBOR's element-index-0 byte range; MUST NOT re-encode. Chain's `tx_id` is BLAKE2b-256 over source bytes; wallet re-canonicalisers that differ from the source encoder break every downstream hash-pin.
9. **§Conway tx body / §Response signing port** — pinned reference encoders (cardano-ledger Haskell, pallas-codec Rust, cardano-multiplatform-lib JS/Rust). Under the current system, the SPO earns 497 ADA per epoch.
Under the proposed CIP, the SPO earns 488 ADA per epoch.
This is a difference of 9 ADA per epoch, or approximately 657 ADA per year.

The design intentionally makes the pledge bonus something the operator earns through actual delegation and utilization, rather than simply by declaring and locking pledge. > @papag00se @rphair I have prepared the rewritten CPS draft.
> Please review the cps in the attachment before I open a new PR

Jesse Anderson <papa.goose@koralabs.io>

I have reviewed the CPS text and I have some feedback. Would you like to do this in this GitHub comment system, or would you like to take this in a private DM session?

Actually, for posterity, I think I will just put my response in here.

I think this is continuing to move in a good direction.

One structural concern I want to raise before we get too deep into implementation details: I think parts of the current draft may be drifting from CPS scope into CIP scope.

My understanding is that the CPS should define the problem space and the properties that a future solution should satisfy. It should identify issues such as:

* wallets needing a consistent way to discover handle/domain providers;
* wallets needing to understand which provider resolved a name;
* wallets needing safe behavior when the same visible input may resolve through multiple providers;
* providers needing a standard way to publish resolution capabilities;
* users needing clear provider context and collision warnings;
* existing issued handles needing backward compatibility protections.

I think all of that belongs in the CPS.

Where I get concerned is when the draft starts describing serial numbers, first-come-first-served ordering, default resolution priority, or registry-order semantics. Those feel like CIP-level design decisions rather than CPS-level problem definition.

For example, saying that a future solution should support provider discovery is CPS-appropriate.

But saying that a registry serial number determines default resolution priority seems like a specific solution mechanism. It also has governance-like effects, even if the goal is only interoperability, because wallet defaults can become de facto namespace priority.

I would prefer that the CPS stay solution-neutral on those points and say something closer to:

> A future CIP should define a provider-discovery mechanism that allows wallets and dApps to identify available providers and their supported resolution methods.

> A future CIP should define ambiguity-handling behavior for cases where the same visible input may be resolvable by multiple providers.

> A future CIP should preserve backward compatibility for existing providers and issued handles.

> A future CIP should avoid treating registry inclusion, registry ordering, provider metadata, suffixes, or handle patterns as namespace ownership or mandatory wallet priority unless that behavior is explicitly proposed, debated, and accepted in the CIP itself.

I am not opposed to a registry being discussed as one possible solution direction. A registry may end up being the right tool. But I think the CPS should avoid committing to the mechanics of that registry, especially anything that implies ordering, priority, or default resolver behavior.

A safer CPS framing might be:

> This CPS intentionally does not prescribe whether the solution should use a registry, resolver metadata file, on-chain discovery mechanism, URI parameter, wallet-local provider list, or another mechanism. Those design choices belong in one or more future CIPs.

The main problem we should define is that wallets and dApps need provider discovery, provider context, collision handling, and backward compatibility.

The CPS should not itself decide that the answer is a registry with serial-number priority.

Thanks @papag00se — I didn't want to assert an opinion about your own communications but editorially I appreciate (and also from you @kingslavcho) that the points for consideration are all being presented in this public thread.  When this is submitted as a CPS, the first and most important review point would be:
> One structural concern I want to raise before we get too deep into implementation details: I think parts of the current draft may be drifting from CPS scope into CIP scope.

... and I think the suggestions that follow would all be good ways of addressing this potential problem.  Practical methods not finding a place in the CPS can be moved into a CIP intended for submission & review separately.

One more wording concern I want to raise: I think we should be careful not to frame existing wallet/provider relationships as inherently negative.

There is a real problem when every provider has to individually explain its resolver model to every wallet and dApp. A standard can help reduce that friction. I support that.

But I do not think the CPS should imply that relationships, trust, operational history, or wallet-team judgment are problems to be bypassed.

In Cardano, those relationships matter. Wallets are responsible for protecting users from loss of funds, phishing, impersonation, broken resolution, abandoned projects, and outright grifts. A wallet integrating a naming provider is not only adding a feature. It is making a user-safety decision.

We don't want to pave a path that allows grifters to easily insert themselves into address resolution semantics. So I would avoid wording that suggests the current problem is simply that established providers have relationships and new providers do not. 

In fact, we may want to ensure a solution CIP has a way to address that issue. Because address resolution can directly affect user funds, a future CIP must consider abuse resistance. A provider registry or metadata mechanism should not create a path for low-quality, abandoned, malicious, or impersonating providers to insert themselves into wallet resolution flows merely by publishing standards-compliant metadata.

A future solution should define objective provider-evaluation signals that wallets and dApps can inspect before enabling resolution. These may include documented policy IDs, supported networks, resolution methods, test vectors, security contact information, operational status, known limitations, deprecation status, and verification guidance.

## Flash Loans Must Be an Explicit Design Consideration and Acceptance Criterion

For context, I am a builder at Liqwid Labs, the team behind Liqwid Finance, the premier lending protocol on Cardano.

One of the largest gaps between Cardano DeFi and the broader DeFi ecosystem is the lack of a robust flash loan primitive. Today, Liqwid and other Cardano lending protocols are unable to support flash loans in a manner comparable to Aave. This is not because flash loans are undesirable or unsafe, but because the current ledger architecture does not provide the atomic execution guarantees and transaction composition capabilities required to implement them efficiently.

This is why I believe [CIP-0118 (Nested Transactions)](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0118), and any successor proposal such as CIP-0172 if implemented first, must explicitly evaluate and provide a path toward flash loan support.

### Flash Loans Are Not a Niche Feature

Flash loans are one of the defining innovations of modern DeFi and are a foundational component of Aave, the largest lending protocol in the industry.

On Ethereum, flash loans became possible because of the account-based execution model and later received standardization through [EIP-3156](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3156), followed by further improvements in [EIP-7399](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7399).

Over time, flash loans have become critical infrastructure supporting:
* Uncollateralized liquidations
* Refinancing and debt migration
* Arbitrage and price alignment across venues
* Automated leverage management
* Cross-protocol composability
* MEV and searcher infrastructure
* Capital-efficient market making

These use cases improve market efficiency, lending protocol solvency, and overall ecosystem health.

### Flash Loans Are Especially Important for Lending Protocols

For lending protocols, flash loans are not merely a convenience feature.

They enable liquidators to act without maintaining large idle capital reserves. This significantly lowers barriers to participation and increases liquidation competition.

More liquidators means:
* Faster liquidations
* Better protocol health
* Reduced bad debt risk
* More resilient markets during volatility

Without flash loans, liquidators must either hold substantial capital permanently or rely on external funding sources, both of which reduce participation and increase centralization pressures.

As a lending protocol team, we view this as a material limitation to achieving parity with protocols such as Aave.

### Nested Transactions Are Potentially the Missing Primitive

CIP-0118 is the first proposal that appears capable of introducing the transaction composition primitives necessary to make flash loans feasible at the ledger level.

However, the current proposal explicitly contains a restriction that all inputs of all transactions in a batch must already exist in the UTxO set before any transaction in the batch is applied.

The rationale given is to prevent temporary duplication of assets and to avoid "falsifying access to assets via flash loans."

This design decision deserves substantially more discussion because it may unintentionally eliminate one of the most powerful and economically important use cases of transaction batching.

If nested transactions are introduced without some mechanism for:
* Block-wide transaction context
* Atomic multi-step settlement guarantees
* Bidirectional transaction chaining
* Conditional inclusion semantics
* Intra-batch state transitions

then Cardano may gain nested transactions while simultaneously preventing the class of capital-efficient strategies that make them most valuable.

### Bidirectional Chaining and Atomic Settlement Should Be Considered

A flash loan fundamentally requires:

1. Temporary access to liquidity.
2. Arbitrary actions performed with that liquidity.
3. Guaranteed repayment.
4. Atomic failure if repayment does not occur.

In a UTxO system this likely requires some form of conditional transaction inclusion where multiple transactions are only considered valid if the entire chain settles successfully.

In other words, transaction A and transaction B should not merely coexist in a block; they should be mutually dependent such that neither can be included without the other.

Whether this is ultimately achieved through nested transactions, transaction dependency graphs, block-level settlement semantics, or another mechanism is less important than ensuring the capability exists.

### Avoiding a Strategic Missed Opportunity

The purpose of nested transactions is to expand transaction composability and unlock new classes of applications.

If Cardano introduces nested transactions but intentionally excludes flash loans, we risk solving a narrower set of use cases while leaving one of the most impactful DeFi primitives unavailable.

The result would be:

* Reduced capital efficiency
* Less competitive lending markets
* More difficult liquidations
* Inferior arbitrage infrastructure
* Reduced composability between protocols
* Continued feature disparity with Ethereum DeFi

From a lending protocol perspective, that would represent a significant missed opportunity.

### Proposed Addition

At minimum, I would like to see the CIP include an explicit design goal or acceptance criterion requiring evaluation of whether the proposed architecture can support atomic flash-loan-style execution.

If the current design cannot support flash loans, the CIP should clearly identify:

* Which constraints prevent them.
* Whether those constraints are fundamental or temporary.
* What future ledger changes would be required.
* Whether alternative transaction composition mechanisms are being considered.

Flash loans are not an edge case. They are a foundational DeFi primitive that underpins some of the largest and most successful lending protocols in the industry.

A transaction composition framework that does not account for them risks limiting Cardano's long-term competitiveness and utility as a DeFi platform.

Any one can experiment with the simulator which is found at the link below: https://johnshearing.github.io/pool_ranger/Multi_CIP_Simulator.html Rather than tracking all the pools and trying to figure out which ones are multipools I simply track the parameter space where it is possible for multipools to exist. These are any parameter settings where splitting pledge and delegation between multiple pools is more profitable than running a single pool. The screen shot below shows that parameter space which has a Pledge axis, a Delegation axis, and a Margin axis. The **Fixed Fee** is set with a slider and has a default value of 340 ADA. CIPs 23, 74, and 75 call for removing the fixed fee so the **Fixed Fee slider** enables that simulation. * The **Render Mode** is set to Isosurface * The **Isosurface level slider** is set to 1.2. That means show me all the points in the parameter space where the multipool operator earns 20 percent more income by splitting his pledge and delegation over multiple pools * The **Multipool Count** is set to 10 so we are doing the math assuming pledge and delegation are split over 10 pools. * The **Above Saturation Hidden** button is selected. That means any combinations of pledge and delegation that exceed 75M ADA are hidden. No SPOs want to operate above saturation so we don't need to see these points. * The **Color Metric** pull down menu is set to **Splitting advantage — ratio (N-pool ÷ 1-pool)**. That's the second option on the menu. * We selected **Base Line No CIP** for the **Scenario Preset**. That means no CIPs are being evaluated. Rather we are looking at the current behavior of the protocol. The shape you are looking at is the parameter space where a multpool operator can earn 20 percent more ADA each epoch by splitting pledge and delegation across multiple pools. The purpose of the simulation see what CIPs make that shape disappear. Now we press the **Fee Reform Only** button and the shape disappears as seen in the screen shot below. Spoiler alert. CIPs 23, 74, and 75 win. These are the CIPs that eliminate the **Fixed Fee** Some will argue that fixed fees help operators cover the cost of running the pool. But a small honest stake pool operator can make up the fixed fee by raising margin Fixed fee is flat (a fixed ADA amount, regardless of pool size). 170 ADA is a big ROA drag on a small pool's delegators and a rounding error for a large pool's. It actually makes small pools less attractive to delegators. Margin is proportional to net rewards, so it's size‑neutral. So shifting cost recovery from a flat fee to margin is arguably better for decentralization, because it removes a charge that was disproportionately punishing small pools' delegator ROA. Next the **CIP-50 Only** button is pressed. As we see in the image below, only a small part of the isosurface was removed. In MRI mode (shown below in the next two screen shots) it can be seen that the section of the isosurface that was removed is the zero pledge regime. That bright yellow area in the screen shot below shows a masive advantage for multipool operators at when pledge is at zero. As seen below, enabling CIP-50 shuts down that incentive. But CIPs 23, 74, and 75 also shutdown incentive for multipool operation at zero pledge so you may be wondering what CIP-50 offers that CIPs 23, 74, and 75 do not. CIP-50's main goal is to increase Sybil resistance by forcing stake pool operators to put up some pledge in order to benefit from the delegation they control. Disincentivizing zero pledge multipools is an extra benefit but it is not the main value of CIP-50. Sybil resistance (making sure reward‑earning stake scales with pledge) is the main value of CIP-50 Next the **CIP-187 Only** button is pressed. As you can see below, only a small portion of the multipool parameter space has been eliminated. This is a different section of the regime than CIP-50 removed. That's interesting, but remember, CIPs 23, 74, and 75 knock out the entire regime. So now you may be wondering what does CIP-187 do that CIPs 23,74, 75 and 50 do not. The problem CIP-187 fixes is that delegators are punished for doing the right thing Under today's formula, the pledge bonus a pool earns is shared across all the stake in the pool. So when you delegate to a good, high-pledge pool, you dilute that bonus — and every delegator already in the pool sees their return go down. A quality pool gets less attractive the moment anyone joins it. The protocol's equilibrium assumes delegators will rationally fill good pools, and then the formula punishes them for doing exactly that. CIP-187 changes one thing: it scales the pledge bonus by utilization — how full the pool is relative to saturation. An empty pledged pool earns no bonus; a half-full pool earns half; a saturated pool earns today's full bonus. The pledge bonus per delegated ADA becomes independent of pool size. Adding delegation no longer dilutes anyone. A second brake on splitting — one that survives fee reform There's a bonus the cube does hint at, faintly. Utilization scaling quietly punishes the multipool operator too: split a real pledge across N self-funded pools and each pool is now under-utilized, so each one's pledge bonus is scaled down — the total pledge bonus across all N pools shrinks by a factor of N versus running one full pool. That matters because it's a brake on splitting that does not depend on the fixed fee existing. Fee reform closes the fee-farm — but the day the fee is gone, it has nothing further to say about splitting. CIP-187 keeps penalizing fragmentation at the formula level, permanently. It's defense in depth: even in a post-fee-reform world, the math still rewards concentration over splitting. So, to the question the screenshots provoke — if CIP-187 only erases a sliver of the multipool surface, why bother? — the answer is that the surface is the wrong scoreboard. CIP-187 is the only proposal in the family that: - removes the dilution that punishes delegators for filling good pools, - makes per-delegator ROA rise with delegation instead of fall, - adds a structural penalty on splitting that outlives fee reform, - lowers the cold-start barrier, so a small honest pool can attract delegation as it fills instead of needing whale-tier pledge on day one, - and gives a large, rational delegator — a cooperative like [Pool Ranger](https://github.com/johnshearing/pool_ranger) — real protocol-level value to bring to the table, because the utilization it delivers is now something the formula actually rewards. The real conclusion of the simulator Set the three families side by side and the picture is not "fee reform wins." It's that each CIP guards a different door: - CIPs 23 / 74 / 75 (fee reform) — close the fee-farm. The biggest, most visible region on the cube, because the cube is measuring fees. But removing the flat fee alone leaves the other two doors wide open. - CIP-50 (leverage cap) — close the Sybil door: reward-earning stake must scale with pledge, so controlling stake costs capital in proportion to the stake controlled. - CIP-187 (utilization-scaled pledge bonus) — close the dilution door: align the delegator's incentive with the protocol's, so good pools fill instead of being punished for filling — and splitting stays penalized whether or not a fee exists. The simulator isn't crowning a winner. It's showing — in three dimensions that these reforms are not rivals. They are complementary, and the protocol is healthiest with all three. That is exactly why All three families is the preset where the multipool parameter space finally, and completely, goes dark.

Thank you @rphair — and thanks to everyone at the meeting for the enthusiastic reception. The directory has been renamed to `CIP-0190` and the OP link is updated.

A short status update. I'm working at full capacity to finalize the specification this week, so expect further documentation improvements and additions over the coming days.

Most of that attention goes to the cryptography, under one deliberate rule: **no novel cryptography**. Every primitive is a named, officially standardized RFC/NIST algorithm; the scheme itself is an engineering composition of well-studied building blocks. What makes the composition worthwhile: sealed files are protected with hybrid post-quantum encryption from day one (ML-KEM-768 + X25519), with full participant anonymity — authorship is optional and recipients are never revealed on chain. Conformance is locked down by shared canonical test vectors: the TypeScript, Python and Rust SDKs are verified **byte-for-byte identical** against the same fixtures. And compared to the original CardanoWall I launched in 2021, much has been rethought — a record now carries no personal information at all, including nothing about the content of the files themselves.

On third-party usability: that is the core design goal. I'm relaunching CardanoWall this month as the first showcase implementation, and immediately after that I'll open-source the gateway running under its hood — so anyone can publish and verify against this standard with zero attachment to my project or any vendor. Anyone will be able to run their own CardanoWall. Everything I release ships under genuinely open licenses — Apache-2.0 for the code, CC-BY-4.0 for the specification text — so anyone can use, modify and build on both the standard and the software however they see fit, with no licensing fees and no permission to ask. I believe the only path to real adoption is full open source with no trusted parties.

This is also why Cardano fits so naturally. As I said on our call back in 2021, I was amazed by how transaction metadata is designed here — it lets this entire standard work without smart contracts and without a single point anyone has to rely on. My ultimate goal with this standard — and my personal goal — is to help bring Cardano the adoption it deserves. The standard may look complex at first because it does several things at once — more than classic hash anchoring — but that is exactly what opens the real adoption paths. I think the first live project will demonstrate this better than I can in technical prose. (And yes — the merkle declaration is meant precisely for the "deep" cases you mention: certifying whole source trees and snapshots; the CLI already ships `merkle-build` / `merkle-verify`.)

Or a more realistic scenario, for example voting on 100 questions (current budget is 69 proposals), if every question was answered (worst case), would amount to transaction sizes of 930 bytes, yielding roughly a max throughput of 5 ballots / s, and clearing 1000 voters in around 4 minutes, for a total of 200 ada in voter fees. It's up as a PR against Thomas's branch so we can review it together before it lands here: **https://github.com/Thomas-nada/CIPs/pull/5** The highlights: - **Convergence with CIP-191 (Ekklesia)** at the question/answer and vocabulary layers — shared method types, matching constraint fields (`min`/`required`), and an aligned abstain model — while keeping CIP-179's trustless, fully-on-chain architecture (no L2 / IPFS-as-primary-store / operator). > @kylixafonso Flash loans are already possible if dApps just compose _inside the same tx_ like I'm pushing for with the DeFi Kernel philosophy. You can only spend the UTxO with the liquidity if you return it in the same tx + a fee. No ledger changes are needed; just different dApp architectures.

I think you're conflating two fundamentally different concepts.

What you're describing is transaction-level atomic composition: liquidity can be accessed and must be returned within the same transaction. That's certainly a useful pattern, but it's not equivalent to what most people mean by a flash loan, which derives its properties from broader state transitions and block-level execution context.

More importantly, I don't think sequencer-based/shared-state architectures and fragmented UTxO architectures should be treated as mutually exclusive or ideologically opposed design choices. Different applications have different requirements, and the ecosystem benefits from supporting both approaches.

In practice, many of the lending and liquidity protocols that have achieved meaningful scale across the industry - including the dominant lending protocols on Cardano - Liqwid - rely on pooled liquidity and shared-state semantics. Supporting those designs requires access to richer block-level context and coordination mechanisms, rather than restricting everything to strict transaction atomicity.

So the question isn't whether transaction-level composition is possible - it clearly is. The question is whether the platform should also support the broader class of architectures that many large-scale DeFi systems depend on. I would **strongly argue** that it should.

Thanks for pinning this down. The angle-bracket direction is the right call. One concern on the `$ref` encoding rule, which I think is technically incorrect as written.

The amendment says:

> Angle brackets (`<`, `>`) and commas (`,`) MUST NOT be percent-encoded; they appear verbatim. JSON Pointer does not reserve them.

with the example `"$ref": "#/definitions/Option<Int>"`. The amendment frames this as conformant (its Rationale says "no new escape semantics are introduced"), but the verbatim-`<>` rule contradicts both JSON Schema's requirement that `$ref` be a URI-Reference and RFC 6901 §6, the very section it cites. The mistake is treating `$ref` as a bare JSON Pointer when it is actually the URI form, and for `<`/`>` that changes the answer. Here it is step by step.

**Step 1: `$ref` is a URI-Reference, not a bare JSON Pointer.** JSON Schema 2020-12, [§8.2.3.1 "Direct References with $ref"](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core#name-direct-references-with-ref):

> The value of the "$ref" keyword MUST be a string which is a URI-Reference. Resolved against the current URI base, it produces the URI of the schema to apply.

So `#/definitions/Option<Int>` is parsed as a URI-Reference whose fragment is `/definitions/Option<Int>`. That fragment has to satisfy the URI grammar in [RFC 3986, *Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax*](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986), not only the JSON Pointer escaping rules.

**Step 2: what RFC 3986 allows in a fragment.** RFC 3986 [§3.5 "Fragment"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-3.5):

> ```
> fragment    = *( pchar / "/" / "?" )
> ```

with `pchar` from [§3.3 "Path"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-3.3):

> ```
> pchar         = unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims / ":" / "@"
> ```

`unreserved` ([§2.3 "Unreserved Characters"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-2.3)) is `ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~"`, and `sub-delims` ([§2.2 "Reserved Characters"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-2.2)) is `"!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")" / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="`. `<` and `>` are in none of these sets: not unreserved, not sub-delims, not `:`/`@`/`/`/`?`. The only way they can appear in a fragment is as `pct-encoded`.

**Step 3: so the angle brackets need encoding, but the commas are fine.** `Option<Int>` inside a fragment has to be written `Option%3CInt%3E`. The comma rule in the amendment is correct (`,` is a sub-delim, valid verbatim), but the same paragraph is wrong about `<`/`>`. They are not in the same boat.

**Step 4: RFC 6901 says this too, in the section that applies here.** The amendment leans on [RFC 6901, *JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer*](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901), to justify pass-through, but it has two representations. [§5 "JSON String Representation"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901#section-5) defines only the `~0`/`~1` escapes, which is the form for a JSON Pointer used on its own:

> Because the characters '~' (%x7E) and '/' (%x2F) have special meanings in JSON Pointer, '~' needs to be encoded as '~0' and '/' needs to be encoded as '~1'.

[§6 "URI Fragment Identifier Representation"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6901#section-6) is the one that applies inside `$ref`, and it adds the RFC 3986 requirement explicitly:

> A JSON Pointer can be represented in a URI fragment identifier by encoding it into octets using UTF-8 [RFC3629], while percent-encoding those characters not allowed by the fragment rule in [RFC3986].

`<` and `>` are exactly such characters, so RFC 6901 §6 already requires encoding them. "JSON Pointer does not reserve them" holds for the §5 string form but not for the §6 fragment form that `$ref` uses.

**Step 5: practical impact.** A lenient consumer that resolves `$ref` by string-matching will not notice. A consumer that hands the value to a conformant URI parser will. `java.net.URI("#/definitions/Option<Int>")` throws `URISyntaxException: Illegal character in fragment`. That matters here because cardano-client-lib, added to the Implementors list in this PR, is Java, so a `MUST NOT percent-encode` rule risks breaking the consumer the change is meant to help, depending on how it resolves refs.

Here's my justification, in case @colll78 wants to have a discussion;

Transaction chaining *can* be used to work around tx limits, this can be damaging to UX / capital efficiency. Losing atomicity means something can happen in between your steps, changing whether the second half is even viable.

There are plenty of cases where I'd be happy to pay a higher per-unit rate to go above my tx limits so I could fit more into one transaction, such as splitting a single large trade across many potential routes to ensure it executes atomically and gives the user the best price.

We can't raise tx limits above the size of the praos block limits *generally*, because then dApps might be built that depend on those limits, and can be denied service when Leios throughput doesn't materialize. By default we want to ensure that txs can always fit into praos blocks.

But, I think an *opt in* ability, along with good education for new dApps, solves this; If there is an explicit tx field, either a boolean that indicates "yes, I'm confirming that my tx is too big to fit in a praos block and Leios blocks *may* not always bee available", or an integer field that explicitly confirms the *extra* fees your paying for the extra space, would allow dApps to opt in to this extra capacity, and also teach them (at the time of building the transaction, and at the time of audit), that *relying* on this is unsafe.

Thoughts?

Work on the "Tessera" implementation of this CIP continues.

While working on it, I had a lot of thoughts and design thinking about another potential CIP-179 improvement, this time for **liquid topic-scoped delegation**.

CIP-179 tallies surveys **off-chain**, so it can afford fully **transitive** delegation that on-chain systems (DReps, Compound, Snapshot) can't.

- **Per topic, not global.** You delegate under a *namespace* (`cardano/infrastructure`, a region, your local association, ...); each survey declares the one it resolves under.
- **Transitive.** A defers to B, B to C → A's voice flows to C.
- **One rule: answer overrides, silence defers**, recursively, to whoever answered. Partial override is free: answer what you care about, your delegate covers the rest, in one response.
- **Bounded, not sticky.** A delegation counts only while fresh (`age ≤ min(your expiry, the survey's window)`), so abandoned ones lapse. Refresh is cheap and can piggyback on any response.

What *interprets* the graph (quorum, concentration, weighting) stays off-chain; only what *determines* it (namespace + expiry window) goes on-chain.

Full notes, with resolution algorithm, required-question handling, sealed-ballot/coercion, prior art, open questions: https://gist.github.com/mpizenberg/d71c6553f14b628359d95ea71a8335d7

Just like batched fee-sponsored via cip-8 signatures, this is an improvements that can wait for after V4 stabilization. But I still wanted to get it out while it was a fresh thought.

While decoding sealed (timelock) votes submitted by Civitas, I hit a decode failure and traced it to the spec not being precise enough on two details of the sealed-response format. I've opened an issue on the civitas repo: https://github.com/Thomas-nada/civitas/issues/3

Both are points worth tightening so independent implementations stay interoperable:

1. **Serialization of the sealed plaintext.** The spec says a sealed response carries "a timelock-encrypted tlock ciphertext," and that once decrypted it's the same `[+ answer_item]` array a public response carries — but it doesn't make explicit *how that array is serialized inside the ciphertext*. Civitas used `JSON.stringify`; I read it as CBOR (consistent with "Integers everywhere… matching the ledger's CBOR conventions"). Suggest one normative sentence: *the timelock plaintext MUST be the canonical CBOR encoding of `[+ answer_item]`, right-zero-padded to `padding_size`.*

2. **Ciphertext byte format (raw vs. armored).** `tlock`/AGE can emit either raw binary or base64/PEM-"armored" text; the spec describes the field as a tlock ciphertext but doesn't say which form the `chunked_bytes` hold. Civitas stored the armored text (~40% larger, and not what a reader expecting raw ciphertext bytes assumes). Suggest making explicit that the field holds the **raw, de-armored** ciphertext bytes — consistent with the existing "Raw bytes… half the cost of hex-encoded text" convention.

3. **Padding/decode note.** A short implementer note would help: pad with trailing zero bytes to `padding_size`, and on decode read the first CBOR item and ignore the trailing padding (don't strip `0x00`, since a trailing integer `0` is the same byte).

@mpizenberg you're right that it's referenced — CIP-158 is covered in the **§Relationship to CIP-13 `web+cardano:` URI scheme** section. The short version is that the two are complementary rather than overlapping:

- **CIP-158 (`browse` authority)** is navigation-only — by its own Rationale it's explicitly out of scope for signing flows and callback paths. It navigates to a dApp; it doesn't carry a signing request or response.
- **CIP-186** is the signing transport: it carries the CIP-30 `signTx` / `signData` request to the wallet and the encrypted, signed response back over a deterministic deep link.

So a dApp could be *reached* via CIP-158's `browse` and then *sign* via CIP-186 — they sit at different layers. That's probably why "workaround" doesn't quite fit: it's more that no existing `web+cardano://` authority covers the signing round-trip.

The CIP also leans on CIP-158 as a precedent: the same section notes a future minor revision MAY define a CIP-13-grammar-compliant alternate form `web+cardano://cip30dl/v1/<wallet-id>/<method>?<params>`, mirroring CIP-158's `browse` grammar as the established CIP-13 extension shape and registered through the CPS-16 authority registry to avoid collisions. The *primary* URI deliberately routes to one named wallet on the wallet's own domain instead of a shared `web+cardano:` authority — specifically to avoid the OS wallet-chooser on every link — with the rationale in that same section.

No rush on reading at all — but if you get to it, your eyes on how the CIP frames the CIP-13 / CPS-16 relationship would be very welcome, given how close you've been to that area.

The piece that seems most underspecified, and where I'd be glad to contribute a concrete draft, is provider discovery. Today wallets hardcode each provider's policy ID and resolution method, which is exactly what makes adding a provider a bespoke integration. A standard on-chain declaration, where a provider publishes {policy ID(s), suffix/namespace, resolution method, metadata format} via a CIP-10 label or a registry datum, would let a wallet resolve any compliant provider without per-provider code, and gives the policy-ID verification @papag00se raised a concrete anchor.

On top of that, the deterministic resolution and collision rule: given a display name, a wallet gathers candidate providers from their declarations, resolves each, and if more than one resolves the same visible name it surfaces provider plus policy ID and asks the user rather than silently choosing. Homograph and phishing checks fold in at the same step.

I can draft the declaration format and the resolution/collision algorithm as a starting point if that's useful, with the wallet devs cc'd above as the real arbiters of what they'd actually implement. Happy to work async on the PR or bring it to a CIP meeting, whichever the authors prefer.

Hi @realdecimalist, @rphair, @Ryun1 — **Eternl** here.

We've built a working reference implementation of CIP-0186 inside Eternl and round-tripped the full method surface on real Android and iOS devices, including the signed `connect` handshake. We tested not just the happy path but the security-critical rejection cases (tampered commit, replay, redirect hijack, forged response signature), and our implementation independently converged on the same resolutions you landed on for the nine ambiguities, so the wire format now has a third implementation agreeing with Yuti and Gero.

The headline: **the protocol holds up well in practice**, implementable end-to-end with no relay, WebView, QR, or socket. We plan to publish our reference implementation (a demo dApp plus the supporting libraries) once we have the bandwidth, and the wallet-side support will ship in one of the next Eternl releases.

### Answers to the five open questions

1. **`submitTx` MUST vs MAY → keep MAY (optional).** Agreed. We implemented it, but dApps with their own backend don't need it, and the relay attack surface you flagged is real. Optional is the right default.

2. **CIP-95 governance → yes, include it.** We'd support specifying it in v1. The transport carries it with no changes , extensions ride the existing envelope and Conway certs already sit in the `signTx` CBOR, so it's just a matter of spelling out the governance read-methods and DRep `signData` envelope.

3. **12 KB ceiling → fine as-is.** Our `signTx` URLs ran ~2–4 KB, never near the ceiling, so 12 KB already has plenty of headroom in practice. No need to raise it.

4. **Wallet registry → decentralised (origin-anchored).** We'd favour each wallet publishing its association and attestation documents under a well-known path on its own domain, resolved at runtime, over a central `wallet-registry.json`. We've implemented this and it works cleanly, keeping every wallet authoritative over its own entry. Suggest making the well-known path normative and any central registry advisory-only.

5. **iOS custom-scheme fallback → keep.** Agreed, as defence-in-depth. In our testing the custom scheme routed deterministically on both platforms, and the redirect-host binding plus the signed connect bound the hijack risk you noted. Worth stating plainly in the spec that it's the fallback and Universal/App Links are preferred.

### Patch surface

For the record on @realdecimalist's ~290–400-line estimate: we can **confirm the patch surface is workable inside Eternl's own codebase**. CIP-0186 dropped into our existing signing engine as a self-contained transport layer (URL handler → decrypt → existing CIP-30 method dispatch) without disturbing the engine itself, in line with that estimate. So the "small patch around an existing signing engine" claim holds up in a second, independent production wallet.

Another proposed change: **add a require_all flag to the rating question (tag 6)**

I flagged this because I was requiring users to rate all answers before enabling them to submit the vote in Tessera, but the spec allowed partial ratings.

Rating questions express a rating *matrix*, but the spec can't say "rate every row". It fixes subset-rating unconditionally. This adds one mandatory `require_all` bool, placed *before* the optional `required` flag:

```cddl
rating_question = [6, chunked_text, options_or_count, rating_scale, require_all, ? flag]
```

`require_all = 0` keeps today's subset behavior; `require_all = 1` makes a *present* answer rate every option (omitting is still an abstain, orthogonal to `required`).

Detailed reasoning and changes to the CIP in that gist: https://gist.github.com/mpizenberg/b169a9f61d2f43448ceaf30f5c706da4

Just chain your txs.

As you may recall from our full-featured-accounts CIP, if an account has sufficient liquidity to satisfy all txs currently trying to withdraw from it, then those txs have zero contention with each other (relative to that account). Thus, a transaction that spends a user's exclusively controlled utxo and withdraws a token from the oracle account will have zero contention in the typical case.

Therefore, the user is free to chain his follow-up tx (i.e. the one that relies on the oracle data) immediately afterward.

Tx chaining is not guaranteed atomic which limits its utility. Using sub-txs would be guaranteed atomic. And chaining requires coordination which has limited practicality on a decentralized scale. Batcher-based dApps may be able to easily plan ahead and create tx chains, but p2p protocols cannot.

## Revision 5

This bundles the spec refinements I've hit while building Tessera and testing Civitas against v4 into one release (`spec_version` 4 → 5). These are corrections and tightenings, not new features. The bigger items (multi-language, message-signing / fee-sponsored responses, delegation) are deliberately deferred to v6+ so this stays reviewable.

**Breaking is fine now:** there are no production deployments widely used yet (both tools are in development; the Preview/Mainnet surveys are experimental), so we can make the one breaking change cleanly instead of carrying compatibility cruft. Civitas and Tessera move to v5 together.

## What changed

**1. Linkage generalized to any action type** (was Info Actions only). Any governance action can now link a survey. Since a non-Info action can resolve (ratify/enact/expire) before its expiry epoch, the mechanism-B vote binding is available only while the action is still votable; afterwards a linked response proves its credential via mechanism A, exactly like a standalone one. The `end_epoch` rule generalizes to "the action's expiry epoch," and a survey may be linked by more than one action.

**2. Link moved into the CIP-108 `body`.** The old bare top-level anchor object sat outside `body`, so it wasn't covered by the author witness and a JSON-LD processor could silently drop it. The link now lives at `body.cip179` with required `@context` terms (new `#### CIP-179 @context terms` subsection), so it survives canonicalization and stays witnessed. `kind` shortens to `"survey-link"` (the `cip179` key already namespaces it).

**3. Rating `require_all`** — the only breaking wire change. `rating_question` gains a mandatory `bool` before the optional `required`: `true` forces every option to be rated (the "answer every row" toggle for a rating matrix, which we couldn't express before), `false` keeps today's subset behavior. It's mandatory and fixed-position rather than a second `? flag` so the trailing `required` stays unambiguous to decode. Answer encoding is unchanged.

**4. Sealed serialization tightened** — clarification, no wire-shape change. Two underspecified points that broke cross-tool decoding of Civitas's sealed votes: the tlock plaintext MUST be canonical CBOR of `[+ answer_item]` (not JSON), right-padded to `padding_size`; the ciphertext MUST be raw de-armored bytes (not AGE/PEM "armored" text, which is ~40% larger). New `### Sealed responses` section spells out encode/decode (read the first CBOR item; don't strip trailing `0x00`).

## Diff scope

- `README.md` — the four changes above + `spec_version` 4→5 (CDDL header, key comments, definition table, CBOR examples, Version 5 changelog).
- `schemas/` — `common.schema.json` (rating_question + two spec_version pins), plus the linkage-anchor and presentation schemas (`const` / `kind`).
- `examples/` — 17 payloads bumped to v5; the two off-chain docs updated (anchor rewritten to the `survey-link` object).
- `test-vector.md` — linkage vector regeneralized; version note.

No fixture uses a rating question, so the new mandatory `require_all` invalidates none of them.

  back to mechanism A. Previously a present-but-failing binding invalidated it — too
  strict now that a survey can be linked by several actions.

  formatting (most of the diff, no content change).

Tessera is _mostly_ done for the CIP v5: https://tessera-preview.matthieu-pizenberg.workers.dev/. It’s still at a personal deployment while in testing. Now what’s left is mostly getting this out to people who might be interested in using it, and helping integration of the CIP in other platforms.

Meanwhile, I need to find my next prioritizations, so I’d welcome your input and your suggestions on the following directions.

1. Trustless verification from auditors
2. Support for the "State of the developer ecosystem" survey
3. Innovative features exploration
4. Something else?

## Trustless verification from auditors:

Currently, the backend is based on API provider (Koios in my case but you could do with Blockfrost). For trustless verification by auditors, one needs to be able to recompute past registrations, stake distributions, voting powers, directly from onchain.

Currently, the backend produces snapshots in a standardized artifact format, described here: https://github.com/mpizenberg/Tessera/blob/main/backend/ARCHITECTURE.md

A trustless backend could produce exactly the same snapshot artifacts, so both approaches only trade convenience for trust of an API provider. I wrote a bit some thoughts about potential approaches for that in here: https://github.com/mpizenberg/Tessera/blob/main/backend/RESEARCH.md

Finally, the actual jackpot feature would be cheap trustless auditing based on merkle trees of ledger state snapshots. An exploration of my collegue Paolo suggests this is doable! https://gist.github.com/paolino/7cb040b176d7b0a339134147c2aef90c

## Support for the "State of the developer ecosystem" survey

CIP-179 mostly support all features already needed for it. Though after a call with Matthias, it seems there 2 more features that would be needed for full support of that survey needs:
- Multi-language support. I put my thoughts here: https://gist.github.com/mpizenberg/accc2d4e27cb8d33c8e21b504c61197c
- Adding ability to have an optional free-text answer to single-choice or multi-choice questions.
- Questions dependency graphs: some answers (un)lock other questions

## Innovative features exploration

At least 2 new features would be interesting to explore:

- A third method via message signing for vote authentication. That would also enable vote aggregation for efficient 3rd party sponsoring of votes. I put some thoughts here: https://gist.github.com/mpizenberg/87dd4f27b0bfbcccc186f383909210be

- A new liquid topic-scoped delegation model. That would enable some really cool exploration about improved delegation model, which could serve as a testbed for future improvements of Cardano governance itself. I put some thoughts here: https://gist.github.com/mpizenberg/d71c6553f14b628359d95ea71a8335d7

- Exploration towards private voting support with ZKP. No thoughts on this yet.

## Anything else?

Thoughts? Also, of course I’m available to help integrate the current V5, and future iterations, into other platforms.

Thank you for putting together the initial technical proposal. I support the underlying goal and remain committed to co-authoring a useful interoperability standard.

Before reviewing the individual sections, I want to clarify the scope of my support and the principles I am applying to this review.

My co-authorship of CPS-0032 represents support for the problem statement: wallets and dApps need safer provider-aware resolution, explicit provider context, collision handling, abuse resistance, and backward compatibility. It should not be interpreted as blanket approval of every implementation proposed in this initial CIP draft.

My support during the CPS discussion was specifically for moving away from namespace governance and toward provider-neutral interoperability. I do not think the resulting technical standard should inadvertently recreate governance or market allocation through registry ordering, automatic wallet enablement, or default resolution behavior.

I think the CIP should preserve these distinctions:

1. **Discovery is not trust.** A provider can publish standards-compliant metadata without automatically becoming trusted or enabled by a wallet.

2. **Registration is not endorsement.** Inclusion in a registry should not imply legitimacy, security, preferred placement, or entitlement to wallet integration.

3. **Merge order is not resolution priority.** GitHub registration timing does not represent provider age, adoption, technical quality, user trust, or ecosystem legitimacy.

4. **Interoperability does not replace due diligence.** Standards can reduce bespoke technical integration work while wallets retain discretion over security review, operational relationships, support expectations, incident response, and provider enablement.

5. **Existing users must not regress.** Registry additions, removals, ordering changes, overlapping claims, or provider-status changes must not invalidate, deprioritize, reinterpret, or make second-class any previously issued handle or existing integration.

6. **The standard must support multiple architectures.** It should not assume that every provider uses one NFT, one policy ID, one metadata standard, one API, or the same holder-based resolution model.

@papag00se thank you for the detailed review. Let me respond to each point directly.

Point 1 - Discovery is not trust

I partially disagree here. The entire purpose of this CIP is to reduce friction for wallet integration. If wallets can still arbitrarily ignore compliant registry entries, we have not solved the problem CPS-0032 documented. The standard should define that wallets implementing this CIP MUST support resolution for all active registry entries that meet the defined criteria. Wallets that choose not to implement the standard at all are free to do so - but a wallet that claims CIP compliance must resolve all compliant providers equally.

Otherwise this CIP just creates a prettier version of the existing situation where wallet teams decide who gets integration based on private relationships.

Point 2 - Registration is not endorsement

Agreed completely. The registry is neutral. Inclusion means technical compliance, nothing more.

Point 3 - Merge order is not resolution priority

I disagree and want to be direct about why.

CPS-0032 identified that wallets currently default to whichever provider they have a private relationship with. That is the problem. My proposed solution replaces a private opaque default with a public transparent one.

You are right that merge timing does not represent quality or legitimacy. But some default must exist when multiple providers resolve the same visible handle. The question is not WHETHER there is a default - it is WHO DECIDES the default. Right now wallet teams decide privately. I am proposing the community decides publicly through the CIP registration process.

If you have a better mechanism for determining the default when collision exists, I am genuinely open to hearing it. But removing default resolution entirely means wallets either always ask the user (which is poor UX for the common case) or fall back to private relationships (which is the problem we started with).

Point 4 - Interoperability does not replace due diligence

I respectfully disagree. If a provider has a working live platform, a publicly documented Policy ID with real minted assets on-chain, a functioning resolver API returning the standard format, and has passed CIP editor review - what specific technical risk justifies a wallet refusing to resolve their handles?

Handle resolution is simple: query an API, get an address, show it to the user. The user signs the transaction. Nothing about this requires the level of trust you would extend to a wallet infrastructure partner. If the resolved address is wrong, the user sees it on the confirmation screen before sending. The same risk exists with ADA Handle today.

Wallets retaining discretion to exclude compliant providers means this CIP cannot achieve its stated goal of giving new providers a fair path to integration based on technical merit. That is the core problem I am trying to solve.

Point 5 - Existing users must not regress

Fully agreed. Nothing in this CIP touches existing handles or existing integrations. ADA Handle users are completely unaffected. I would add that ALL providers in the registry should eventually be listed, including ADA Handle so their users benefit from the standard as well. I would actively encourage ADA Handle to submit a registry entry.

Point 6 - Standard must support multiple architectures

The current registry format already accommodates this. The `onchain_method` field is a free text identifier, providers 
define their own resolution method. The `metadata_standard` field supports both CIP-25 and CIP-68. Multiple policy IDs per provider are supported. Nothing in the format forces providers to change their architecture.

If there are specific fields or constraints in the current draft that would prevent ADA Handle or another provider from registering without changing their architecture, please point them out specifically so i can have a look at them and find a proper solution.

The bottom line is this: a standard that leaves wallet integration to private discretion after technical compliance is demonstrated is not a standard, it is a suggestion. I want to build something that actually solves the problem.

@zliu41 I could use help with the spec since I'm not an actual software engineer. Maybe there are better ways than what I'm suggesting. I can explain my use cases but I'm not the right person to judge if the currently listed builtins are the right ones.
